This novel concept has several applications and has allowed the introduction of a new equation - the nonuniform associative Yang-Baxter equation. This new equation possesses a number of unique properties and is associated with various sequences of two-sided ideals in a quasitriangular algebra. It is also discovered that the two-sided ideals in a quasihomogeneous coalgebra satisfy this new equation. Furthermore, a connection between the nonuniform associative Yang-Baxter equation and generalized factorization property in quasigroups has been established. Lastly, a number of examples have been developed to illustrate the concept of two-sided ideals in a quasitriangular algebra and the nonuniform associative Yang-Baxter equation. These examples include two-sided ideals in algebra of 3-dimensional vectors and a nonuniform associative Yang-Baxter equation depending on a parameter in shape of 3-dimensional vector. It is clear that the concept of two-sided ideals in a quasitriangular algebra is a powerful tool for the study of quasigroups and the newly developed nonuniform associative Yang-Baxter equation offers a novel method for the investigation of quasigroups. It is anticipated that the concept of two-sided ideals in a quasitriangular algebra and the nonuniform associative Yang-Baxter equation will be of use in the study of ribbon structures in quasigroups. Formal verification through Hoare logic is a well-established approach to
assessing the reliability of software programs.  However, this method faces
a significant hurdle in obtaining precise pre- and post-condition
descriptions for programs.  The present work aims to overcome this
challenge by utilizing linguistic techniques to generate reliable pre- and
post-condition descriptions from high-level descriptions in logical forms
that capture the program's intended behavior.  The integration of Hoare
logic and linguistic modeling through nonmonotonic description logics
enables us to define conditions and query the program's domain
consistently, based on its output results.  The developed proof-of-concept
combines state-of-the-art linguistic tools, including Paragram and DLvTime,
to express specifications and define Hoare logic axioms, and demonstrates
its effectiveness with a number of simple programs.  The documentation for
this method, along with sample specifications, are accessible online at
https://github.com/fpcochard/natural-hoare.  Ultimately, this research
investigates the potential for leveraging linguistic structures to formally
define the domain and specifications for programs, and we discuss its
limitations as well as potential extensions for broadening its utility.  The
present work constitutes the initial effort in integrating linguistic
techniques with Hoare logic, and we anticipate that further advancements
could lead to more robust methods for extracting reliable specifications from
natural language descriptions.  The present study was conducted with support

Distributed consensus is crucial for various distributed systems, such as distributed databases and blockchains, to function correctly. The Canopus protocol efficiently manages large-scale distributed consensus without the need for a single leader, achieving this through a self-balancing tree structure that allows Canopus to recover from failures and malicious behavior. The new Canopus variant, RCanopus, continues to outperform other consensus protocols, specifically in the direction of efficiency, by using a fault-tolerant approach based on graph theory to handle failures and malicious behavior. Furthermore, RCanopus can recover from various types of failures and attacks, such as up to t+1 failures, network delays, and Byzantine attacks, where t represents the number of tolerated failures. Despite its resilience, RCanopus maintains a simple design and achieves optimal performance by utilizing logical graph structures and conservative input handling. The performance of RCanopus is confirmed through various failure and attack tests, showcasing its ability to handle diverse scenarios while ensuring the consistency of the distributed consensus. Recent studies employing neutron spin echo spectroscopy have yielded conflicting results regarding the impact of cholesterol on the bending modulus of lipid membranes. Some research suggests that cholesterol increases the bending modulus, while other studies indicate a minimal effect. We attempt to reconcile these findings by re-examining the electrical field effect on lipid membranes in the presence of cholesterol. Our analysis reveals that an application of an electric field can reduce the modulus or introduce inhomogeneities with lower modulus values. Considering that cholesterol can impede water penetration, we propose that the apparent increase in bending modulus observed in previous studies could be a result of an electric field effect rather than an inherent property of cholesterol. Furthermore, we explore the notion that membrane regions containing bound cholesterol may exhibit lower mechanical stability compared to those without. Supportive of this idea, our calculation reveals that sites of cholesterol binding can actually decrease the modulus or introduce inhomogeneities with lower modulus values. Consequently, we strive to provide a more accurate interpretation of recent experimental findings indicating that the presence of cholesterol may reduce the bending modulus or create more flexible areas within the membrane. Our analysis ultimately provides further evidence of membrane liquid-liquid phase transitions in fully hydrated lipid cholesterol systems and suggests that these phases exhibit a considerable range of moduli values. Depending on the specific membrane composition and conditions, these variations can occur over a considerable scale, potentially influencing the membrane's mechanical behavior and functionality. Notably, our analysis reveals that applying an electric field can induce phase transitions or create inhomogeneities within membranes that were previously considered to be relatively uniform and stable, such as those comprised of POPC and DOPC with low cholesterol content. These results emphasize the significance of considering various factors like fatty acid chain length, water content, temperature, electric field conditions, and cholesterol population when studying membrane structure and its relationship with lipid composition. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that applying an electric field can induce phase transitions or create inhomogeneities within membranes that were previously considered to be relatively uniform and stable, such as those comprised of POPC and DOPC with low cholesterol content. These results imply the existence of membrane inhomogeneities on a considerable scale, which can influence biological membrane functionality and processes such as endocytosis and signal transduction. Our analysis provides a more accurate interpretation of recent experimental findings indicating that the presence of cholesterol may reduce the bending modulus or create more flexible areas within the membrane. These results validate theoretical models suggesting that cholesterol can decrease the mechanical stability of these areas, which in turn can introduce liquid-liquid phase transitions in biological membranes.

Our research demonstrates that certain cosmological models, including black holes, neutron stars, and the Big Bang, can be accurately explained by loop quantum mechanics. We derived the Hamiltonian for loop quantum gravity using the Arnowitt-Deutsch-Misner formalism and subsequently obtained the corresponding equations of state. By applying these equations to relativistic stellar models, we found that they predict mass-loss phenomena for both black holes and neutron stars at certain critical densities, and also briefly considered a potential link between loop quantum gravity and the inflation theory. Our findings reveal that they are consistent with established astrophysical observations of compact star behavior. Additionally, we identified notable similarities and differences between predicted behavior and experiments involving the GRANATA device, which demonstrates quantum effects under high acceleration. Finally, we explored the potential meaning of certain features in the neutron star spectrum that were previously attributed to gravity-like quantum effects. Our research indicates that it is possible that the gravitational field, rather than other areas of study, may serve as a means of testing quantum mechanics in inanimate objects. Our model also predicts certain characteristics of black hole and neutron star behavior that have yet to be independently verified. Advanced deep-learning-based object detectors have achieved superior performance in challenging computer vision tasks but often lack reliable quantification of their uncertainties. A novel object detection method called BayesOD is presented, designed to address this issue by generating accurate uncertainty maps. By integrating a Bayesian treatment of a widely employed Region of Interest regressor, BayesOD achieves high uncertainty prediction results. Performance is further enhanced with a collaborative representation approach, demonstrating improved prediction and representation abilities. Experimental evaluations using Standard Train/Test, Cross-View, and Partial Domain datasets showcase BayesOD's capability to effectively assess and reduce sampling bias, demonstrating superior uncertainty detection and robustness against domain shifts. Notably, BayesOD surpasses existing deep-learning-based detectors and uncertainty assessment models across multiple uncertainty metrics on the CUILabel dataset. Furthermore, BayesOD exhibits superior adaptability when applying domain adaptation techniques to respond to varying uncertainty levels. A comprehensive open-source code and thorough experimental guide are provided to facilitate replication of the study's findings. Comprehensive performance assessments and ablation analyses on representative datasets and models reveal that BayesOD's success is due to the integration of two key techniques: collaborative regression function for accurate target embedding generation and accurate uncertainty assessment, and Bayesian regression for reliable sample embedding generation and accurate uncertainty assessment. Notably, BayesOD's performance outshines competing two-stream detectors that attempt to achieve accurate uncertainty assessment, highlighting the effectiveness of the two proposed techniques. Finally, performance studies reveal that BayesOD achieves superior outcomes when applied to diverse computer vision tasks, empowering these networks with reliable uncertainty assessment capabilities. Results of the study indicate that BayesOD's performance is in sync with the complexity of the network architecture, exhibiting a strong correlation between the two factors. Consequently, the study demonstrates the practical utility of the study's findings, inspiring the exploration of other network architectures with varied design principles. A duplicate version of the code is hosted at the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/strl-group/BayesOD.

The prediction of traffic dynamics is crucial for operating motorways efficiently. In this study, we investigate the potential for using machine learning to make accurate predictions about traffic flow, given a historical dataset of the motorway's moving segments. In particular, we use advanced deep learning models to identify patterns in both spatial and temporal data, and demonstrate the effectiveness of a combined approach for forecasting traffic flow. Our findings indicate that these models outperform a established shallow machine learning method, while also highlighting the challenges of predicting traffic on specific lanes. Unlike previous research, we address the prediction challenge as a multi-output problem, where the class of moving segments and the associated traffic dynamics are simultaneously predicted. In addition, we explore the use of undersampling for balancing the distribution of samples in the training dataset, since the class imbalance significantly affects the performance of traffic flow prediction models. Our results show that these models can be used to make online predictions during a longer period than the models used in previous studies, providing information that is essential for real-time motorway management. Finally, we discuss the possibilities of extending these methods to sequences of frames, rather than single frames, in order to improve the accuracy of traffic flow prediction. In 1969, R.W. Gray introduced the concept of Gray classes in relation to rewriting systems, which has significant implications for reaching consistency in such systems. A rewriting system is considered consistent if it has a unique normal form and can be in one of three states: normal form, never reaching normal form, or unreachable. We revisit Gray's work and provide an alternative,equivalent definition focusing on the structure of the rewriting system itself, rather than the form of reducibility used in the original study. We also introduce a method for rewriting within Gray classes and demonstrate its potential applications in achieving consistency for a particular type of rewriting system. Specifically, we show that a parallel composition of monoidals, which are type of weighted rewriting system, is consistent if and only if it meets certain conditions on the weights. We utilize Gray classes to establish that such conditions are indeed necessary and sufficient for consistency in this context. Furthermore, our method for rewriting in Gray classes aligns with the concept of Gray paths, which are used in the original study. We also identify an error in the prior research, which involved a misinterpretation of the notion of Gray classes for never-reducible systems. We correct this mistake by demonstrating that, in fact, the Gray classes for never-reducible systems do not exist. Building on this insight, we show that, in the context of a particular type of rewriting system known as sequential, the condition of never-reducibility can be characterized precisely through the non-existence of Gray classes. We also achieve consistency in the sequential case by employing a different rewriting criterion, which we refer to as weak closure. We align our approach with the concept of partial order, which is closely related to the notion of reducibility, by defining it through a corresponding binary relation. In the context of a particular type of rewriting system known as parallel composition, the condition of weak closure can be characterized precisely through the non-existence of Gray classes. We also achieve consistency in the parallel composition case by employing a different rewriting criterion, which we refer to as closure under composition. We demonstrate that, in the context of a particular type of rewriting system known as parallel composition, the condition of closure can be characterized precisely through the non-existence of Gray classes. We also achieve consistency in the parallel composition case by employing a different rewriting criterion, which we refer to as closure. We demonstrate that, in the context of a particular type of rewriting system known as parallel composition, the condition of closure can be characterized precisely through the non-existence of Gray classes. Convolutional neural networks have become widely successful in a broad range of image recognition challenges, from natural image classification to more complex applications like medical image analysis. In the case of neuroimaging, convolutional networks play a vital role in decoding the hidden configurations of brain structures, especially when working with 2D representations of transverse brain scans. This paper introduces a novel method for segmenting hippocampi in Alzheimer's and epilepsy images by employing Multiple Convolutional Neural Networks (MCNN) in addition to providing an exegesis on enhancing hippocampus segmentation in MCNN frameworks. We have conducted a comprehensive evaluation of our method using a publicly accessible dataset hosted on Kaggle, comparing our results with other established techniques. Our results demonstrate that our approach surpasses the performance of Tandon et al. and Jia et al.'s methods, with a macro average dice coefficient of 0.7521 and dice coefficient of 0.9086 for left and right hippocampus and earbud regions, Jia et al. achieved an average dice coefficient of 0.6641 and dice coefficient of 0.5991 for left and right hippocampus regions, Tandon et al. achieved an average dice coefficient of 0.6851 and dice coefficient of 0.5701 for left and right hippocampus regions, while earbud added around 4% to the performance of the two former methods. We have also analyzed the corresponding class-weight mapping for better understanding of the class differences. This research introduces a new method for hippocampus segmentation in MCNN frameworks, showcasing its effectiveness in a multi-class segmentation problem with remarkable results, outperforming previously established techniques. Additionally, we present a novel interpretation of the class differences, providing valuable insights for experts in the field of neuroimaging and brain analytics. This research is expected to contribute to the accelerated and accurate manual labeling of hippocampus and earbud regions in Alzheimer's and epilepsy studies. Such advancements in automated segmentation could lead to more efficient data compilation for deeper epidemiological studies and a better comprehension of Alzheimer's and epilepsy diseases. Our research identifies the Cosmic Ray Albedo Neutron Decay (CRAND) as the primary factor producing high-energy particles at low Earth orbit. A comprehensive Monte Carlo model has been developed to simulate these particles and their influence on atmospheric events at low Earth orbits. By using this model, we calculated the number of these particles at low Earth orbits and found it to be significantly higher than expected. Our calculations show that at an altitude of 400 km, the number of particles generated per second exceeds 10^6, with 80% being electrons, gamma rays, and neutrons, and the remainder being protons and alpha particles. Additionally, we conducted a statistical analysis of the model's outcomes and found that 85% of these particles fall within a 50 km radius of the orbit. By utilizing the model to simulate multiple orbits, we observed significant variations in the number of particles at the orbit's extremities, with the potential number of particles ranging from 5.8x10^5 to 1.2x10^6 particles per second. Our simulations also demonstrate that the distance from the Sun affects the number of particles, with the potential number of particles at low Earth orbits being twice as high in opposition as in conjunction. By using the model to simulate an ISS event, we verified that the experimentally observed number of particles matches the expected outcome. In conclusion, our model's outcomes align with experimental data and provide a comprehensive understanding of the CRAND effect, with the model being a valuable tool for explaining and predicting this phenomenon at low Earth orbits. The strength of the CRAND effect relies on several factors, including the location of the observer relative to solar conditions, making it a crucial factor for multiple applications such as spacecraft design, radiation medicine, and atmospheric physics. Our model offers a significant contribution to these fields and can serve as a valuable resource for multiple areas of research. With the advancement of space technology and the establishment of various bases on planets and moons, understanding the CRAND effect may become essential for their survival and operation. Our simulation outcomes can serve as a starting point for future research and may need adjustment or expansion to accurately reflect various scenarios or locations. Notably, our model's limitations lie in its inability to accurately simulate deep space particle production, with the model requiring further development or modification to accurately capture this phenomenon. Additionally, our model's convergence of results requires further time and computational power to accurately simulate various scenarios, with the model's current processing time exceeding several days for multiple orbits, with the number of particles reaching 10^6

Recently, a technique known as Differential Privacy has gained attention for concealing data in low-rank matrices, particularly through low-rank matrix fulfillment. This study explores a crowdsourcing framework for completing low-rank matrices on a per-row basis, similar to previous applications. To protect user contributions from being linked, we implement a Differential Privacy method which adapts the Huber loss function for this specific purpose. This approach utilizes an optimization procedure with the Huber loss function, incorporating both matrix completion and regularization, thereby protecting user data. To validate the effectiveness of this method, we implemented two iterations of the algorithm using synthetic and MD5 summary data of Wikipedia articles and Amazon product reviews, evaluating its ability to meet the matrix completion and Differential Privacy goals. These experiments demonstrated that two iterations of the algorithm are necessary to fulfill these goals while maintaining accuracy. Furthermore, a comparison with a commonly used method confirmed that our method not only fulfills these goals but also delivers better accuracy. This study not only contributes to the development of a novel low-rank matrix fulfillment method but also provides a framework for understanding the Huber approach in this specific context. This framework offers a potential solution for protecting user data while completing low-rank matrices on a per-row basis. You can access the source code at https://github.com/malhki/Huber_DPFM. Additionally, a technical report providing further details on this method can be found at https://doi.org/10.5281/ten Thousand.pdf.

We have developed an expanded version of our astrodust model that accurately predicts the extinction, emission, and polarization of light in the UV to mid-IR range. This revised model takes into account large grains that are not typically present in the interstellar medium and also includes the effects of light polarization by aligned polar dust grains. The polar dust grains form through a process that involves the attraction of negatively charged grains in the wake of highly charged polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, which have a significant influence on their alignment. The model relies on six free parameters, including the size of grains in the small and large categories, the exponential cutoff energy for grain extinction, the distance between grains, the size of substructures within grains, and the electron density of PAHs. Located approximately 30 astronomical units from its host star, the planet has a mass equivalent to that of Jupiter and sits at a location where gravitational influence is critical in shaping the disk's structure. Compared to similar disks, CIDA 1's disk exhibits unusual ring-like patterns and increased mass near the inner disk region, which can be attributed to the host star's effect. Models of dust evolution have been applied to analyze possible configurations that could result in the observed luminosity and spectral energy distribution of CIDA 1's disk, taking into consideration carbon-doped glasses as the absorber responsible for its spectral features. According to these models, a massive planet with mass similar to Jupiter can exist, which not only influences the disk's pressure but also produces wave actions that transfer angular momentum and shape the disk's density and azimuthal velocity. These dynamical effects have been found to be necessary in explaining observed disk structures and variability, such as ring features and wave patterns, which cannot be accounted for by static disk models alone. As a result, presence of a massive planet at similar mass ratios to the host star has been detected in disks surrounding very low-mass stars, which may have significant implications for planetary formation theories. Moreover, a new type of planetary effect on disk structure has been identified and proposed, which can lead to ring formation through planet-induced density waves, particularly in low-mass star systems. These findings also imply that dynamical mass transfer from the planet could be a major source of mass flow rate, which may have significant consequences for other observed low-mass star disk features. Furthermore, this discovery has also led to the suggestion that massive planets may exhibit shorter or equal lifetimes compared to their non-massive counterparts. These planetary features have also been proposed as potential targets for investigating the dynamics and chemistry in planetary systems surrounding very low-mass stars in the future. Finally, a new theory on how massive planets can affect the evolution and longevity of solid ring structures have also been suggested, which can potentially last millions of years or more as long as the planet remains gravitationally dominant over the system. These findings have also been taken into consideration for future observations of CIDA 1's disk in Kuiper belt-like submillimeter continuum using NOIRSource. A few recent studies have adapted a variational image partitioning model that assigns distinct regions in an image to distinct clusters. However, such a model faces problems during data sparse representation due to its over-smooth nature. In our proposed model, image partitioning and image reconstruction constraints are seamlessly integrated, and it exploits the strengths of both sparse image reconstruction and image partitioning methods. This research explores the concept of static analysis through Abstract Interpretation, a method that relies on pre-defined abstract domains to approximate program behaviors. Traditional numerical domains advance in steps: initial lower and upper estimations are established for each program variable, with these values always rising or falling simultaneously. Our innovation is a domain where these processes can unfold at different rates, allowing for tighter precision. A key challenge lies in guarantee that the analysis remains sound. We've discovered new techniques for "storing" accuracy within numerical structures, much like operators do. A key property of our constructed domains is "consistency," with consistently rising or falling values that do not worsen program behavior approximations. We've developed a new set of calculus rules for operating on these domains, with the domain's "monotonicity" ensuring that the analysis remains sound. An existing program analysis with the conventional climbing approach was applied to the language with bounded array access, using our new, incrementally constructed domains to attain soundness. Our experiments show that the resulting static analyzer outperforms the original one, both in terms of precision and in terms of computation time. We firmly believe that this breakthrough offers significant potential for further improvements in static analysis. An accompanying technical report provides even more in-depth details on our research.  A practical tool implementing these ideas is available for download at https://bitbucket.org/sofamlab/ai-falling-phase. Topological phonons are crucial in understanding topological electronic properties of materials. Topological phonon excitations are predicted to preserve topological characteristics, thereby determining the topological electronic structure. Theoretical studies have demonstrated the presence of topological phonons in insulating materials with strong spin-orbit coupling, especially in baryons. However, generating and controlling topological phonons in these materials is highly challenging. To investigate topological phonons in insulating ceramics, we employed ab initio calculations and found that topological phonons exist in certain ceramic perovskites with and without antiferromagnetic order. By using dynamic stability criteria based on the mechanical response and anharmonicity, we identified limited cases of dynamic and metastable topological phonons. The presence of topological phonons in these materials is independent of temperature and magnetic order and is regulated solely by the electronic structure of the insulator. Moreover, we discovered that electromagnetic radiation can convert normal phonons into topological phonons, thus activating topological phonon excitations. Through these findings, we demonstrate the excitations of topological phonons in insulating ceramic perovskites through theoretical predictions and identify new applications of topological phonons in insulating systems. The existence of topological phonons in insulating systems may lead to new understanding of the nature of topological phonons in superconducting and magnetic materials. Furthermore, we anticipate the potential observation of topological phonons in insulating ceramic perovskites through experimental techniques such as infrared spectroscopy and atomic-scale imaging. Our study demonstrates the excitations of topological phonons in wide varieties of materials with significant implications for the advancement in the field of topological phonons. Notably, we demonstrate the regulated conversion of normal phonons into topological phonons through electromagnetic radiation, thereby opening new avenues for the manipulation and control of topological phonons. The significant implications of our study for the advancement in the field of topological phonons, particularly in regulating topological phonons with electromagnetic radiation. As a slender mirror approaches a moving atom, it interrupts the particle-antiparticle pair's circular time path, forcing the atom to deviate from its straight motion. Consequently, the atom acquires a temporary circular motion trajectory. During the encounter, the atom's velocity and the circular force it experiences result in emitted electromagnetic radiation, and its energy increases due to the circular force. This increase in energy is transient and eventually dissipated as the circular force wears off. A similar phenomenon occurs when the atom collides with a slender mirror, but an energy loss rather than gain occurs. This collaborative and conflicting movement of the atom and the mirror produces a variety of electromagnetic emissions characterized by distinct time patterns, depending on whether the forces are reinforcing or opposing each other. These results imply that an atom can emit light long after the encounter or collision has ended, producing a long-lasting electromagnetic effect. Furthermore, when a slender mirror moves at high speeds near an atom, it excites the atom, causing it to jump into a higher energy state. Upon the mirror's passage, the atom returns to its original energy level, resulting in an energy loss equal to the circular force it experienced while in the higher energy state. This phenomenon is analogous to the Landau-Khalatnikov-Zubok effect, in which an impurity is activated when it interacts with a high-speed sound wave. We have also demonstrated that electromagnetic emissions resulting from these encounters can be a primary source of radiation and may be observable from distant atoms, providing a new means of observational interaction between moving slender mirrors and atoms. These theoretical predictions could potentially be verified through experimental manipulation of nanoscale objects. A comprehensive mathematical framework for these phenomena as described in the book "Radiation from Moving Object-Atom Interactions, with Comprehensive Template Approach" is available and outlined in Chapter 9. This framework is further applied in Chapter 11 to estimate the electromagnetic emissions resulting from various relativistic slender mirror-atom encounters and their potential observability. In graph fair learning, we aim to develop a model that accurately predicts node labels while ensuring that groups of connected nodes have similar chances of being correctly labeled. Building on the concept of localized fairness introduced by Ghasemi et al. in 2020, we propose a new framework for graph fair learning, which uses a two-stage approach involving the detection of community structures and the training of fair models based on those structures. However, we find that localized fairness suffers from the same problems as its global counterpart, including the risk of biased label distribution and the loss of information due to model average pooling. To improve the fairness of models in the localized setting, we develop a new method that uses the proximity of connected nodes as a measure of their label similarity. This leads to the introduction of two new fairness metrics, MLCF and MLCFd, which incorporate the graph structure into the definition of localized fairness, and our algorithm, LCF-GNN, which uses the detection of community structures and the training of GNN models based on those structures to achieve better prediction accuracy and fairness without bias. Our study, however, reveals that MLCFd leads to the loss of useful information, and we find that LCF-GNN using the simple pooling method suffers from the same problems as its global counterpart, and its accuracy depends on the strength of the graph structure, and its performance can be bettered by the methods that use the same structure in the top-down approach, such as TopDown-GNN, SelfTrain, and ReWeight. We also introduce a new re-weighting approach that is based on the detection of community structures, which improves the accuracy of models by distributing correctly labeled nodes evenly across the graph. Our study shows that the re-weighting approach, called RW-LCF, outperforms its counterparts in the accuracy of models, and its effectiveness can be further improved in the accuracy of models by the methods that use the same structure in the top-down approach, such as TopDown-GNN, SelfTrain, and ReWeight. This study raises the question of why there is a need for the two-stage approach when the fairness of models in the localized setting can be improved by the methods that use the same structure in the top-down approach, and it suggests that the localized concept may not be much better than the global concept after all. This research focuses on developing and implementing a method of successive approximations for a class of non-linear convolution equations arising from the description of reversible enzyme reactions using macroscopic kinetic equations. We derive an equation for the concentration of enzyme-substrate-substrate complexes and utilize the equation to determine the reaction rate and equilibrium constants, along with key parameters such as substrate concentration, reaction rate, and equilibrium constants. To solve the equation, we propose a method of successive approximations and provide a convergence proof, showing that the method converges to a unique solution. We also present an alternative method using the Newton-Raphson algorithm to iteratively solve the equation, and demonstrate its effectiveness with numerical examples. Additionally, we analyze the algorithm's stability using the linearization of the equation and show that it satisfies certain conditions for stability, further validating its use in practical applications. We verify the accuracy and practicality of our algorithm with numerical examples involving reaction rate and equilibrium constants calculations. We also use our algorithm to analyze enzyme reactions with multiple steps and degrees of freedom and generate corresponding phase portraits. Furthermore, we apply our algorithm to a specific case of hexokinase reaction and demonstrates its utility in practice. We analyze the algorithm's performance using leading term asymptotics and stability analysis with the fast scale limit, and demonstrate its reliability on various platforms including MATLAB and VKTEACH. We also address the limitations and assume that our algorithm can be adapted and applied to other related problems such as photosynthesis with proper modifications. This research centers around the missing transverse momentum (p_~S) in the final state, where points of interest fall into two categories: those with p_~S below 120 GeV, denoted as S1, and those with p_~S above 150 Geve, denoted as S2. In the S1 region, excesses over the standard model's background are discovered in four distinct variables at 95% confidence level (CL): they appear in combinations of top quark jet multiplicity, transverse momentum, and tau-lepton jet multiplicity, reaching CLs of 78.1, 83.6, 49.6, and 73.5 respectively. In regions of higher p_~S (S2), no notable excesses over the standard model's background are found, which could be interpreted as disjoint regions of supersymmetry that require distinct particle production mechanisms due to their position relative to a threshold at p_~/~S = 150 GeV. In a simultaneous fit to data across all variables, we find a combined best-fit point, where point S1 combines with a disjoint interpretation of data at point S2, yielding a best-fit cross-section at 13 TeV of 58.2 fb, accompanied by a best model fit that includes a point S1 best-fit cross-section of 79 fb and a best-fit point S2 cross-section of 49 fb. Review-based product recommendations have been widely used to enhance customer engagement and sales. The key to success in this field lies in identifying the most relevant and trustworthy reviews that can accurately reflect customers' needs. Although existing techniques have focused on modeling review messages in isolation, they fall short due to the insufficiency of contextual information and inconsistent writing styles in reviews. To address these limitations, this paper introduces Sentiment-sensitive Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN) which aims to dynamically weigh the contextual and semantic contributions of individual words and full sentences in reviews. Specifically, the proposed method employs an interactive mechanism to represent multi-aspect sensitive review information through sentence-level attention, leveraging contextual clues to provide dense representation of full sentences. Additionally, the network incorporates a sentiment-sensitive channel to adaptively combine the two representations according to the sentiment cues in reviews. Experimental results on three real-world datasets show that SIFN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines with an improvement of 2.18% or more in recommendation accuracy and MRR scores. The method's performance is due to its ability to identify the most relevant and trustworthy reviews in diverse writing styles and contextual information in reviews. Notably, the proposed method achieves better performance in datasets with more prominent sentiment-oriented characteristics. Evaluation results further demonstrate the effectiveness of the intrinsic evaluation in assessing the performance of different sentence-level attention mechanisms and the extrinsic evaluation in identifying the most relevant and useful reviews in real-world scenarios. training outcomes. Nevertheless, researchers are divided on the most effective way 
to implement this method. While some studies have achieved notable success with 
synthetic data generated through character-level manipulation, others have reported 
favourable results with sentence-level data generated through meaning-preserving 
modifications. We contend that a thorough examination of the factors influencing 
data augmentation methods' performance is needed. In our research, we explore the 
significance of lexical substitutions in determining the quality of data augmentation 
for BS-AR-EN through a comprehensive experiment design. We evaluate the impact of 
words to translate, lexical substitutions, sentence length, and translation quality 
on the translated sentence's fluency and accuracy by using the BLEU metric as our 
target variable. We employ the Bayesian Average Likelihood Estimation method to 
gather more accurate word-level predictions. Our results indicate that words to 
translate have the greatest influence on BLEU score, followed by lexical 
substitutions, sentence length, and translation quality. We also demonstrate that 
using experts to select lexical substitutions enhances BLEU score in comparison to 
random substitutions. Notably, our research shows that sentence-level data 
augmentation can yield better results than character-level augmentation, which is 
consistent with previous studies. We contribute towards developing a method to 
automatically select lexical substitutions by translating a source sentence using

the translation as fluent or disfluent. We also conduct an exhaustive search to 
determine the best set of lexical substitutions and demonstrate that utilizing 
fluency-annotated data from existing resources or crowdsourced can be effectively 
used to implement this method. Ultimately, we apply our approach to translate Arabic- 
English code-switched text and verify that it enhances the translated text's 
fluency and accuracy. Our source code is available for review at https://github.com/dkowalski/LexSubBSAREN.

We also offer an explicit interpretation of connectable branes in lambda deformations and derive necessary and sufficient conditions for their connectability in both classical and generalized settings, and we use these results to identify Coxeter graphs whose local generalized lambda deformations allow for connectable branes. Our findings have practical applications in higher-spin theories and string theory, particularly in the GS and NSR formulations of string theory in light of recent developments on lambda deformations' impact on bosonization. Using the example of a non-Abelian Wilson line, we also explore how generalized lambda deformations can arise from non-Abian T-duality. To achieve accurate analytical converter design, it is crucial to incorporate delay considerations into the analytical models. This requirement becomes even more profound when designing converters for high-speed applications. Researchers have developed various sparse-model frequency-dependent macromodeling methods that account for propagation delays. These models can be generated using the parameter estimation tool in MatLab's Curve Fitting Toolbox, which is shown to effectively produce reliable sparse models for complex analog converters operating at high frequencies. This research demonstrates that the application of the Genetic Algorithm in matLab's Global Optimization tool can be used to further refine and optimize the accuracy of the sparse models obtained. This optimization allows the Genetic Algorithm to fine-tune the distribution of the model's coefficients, resulting in significant improvements to the model's accuracy. This optimization can significantly contribute to reducing the inaccuracies associated with the models, which is particularly crucial in designing analog converters for use in high-speed applications. This paper presents a comprehensive review of the conventional methods for analytical converter design, with a focus on delay consideration, in addition to introducing a novel and efficient technique that utilizes the Genetic Algorithm to optimize the models' accuracy. We have utilized the conventional vector error reduction method, in conjunction with the MatLab's Curve Fitting Toolbox's least square error minimization, to develop the models. Furthermore, to prove the efficacy of the proposed optimization technique, we have applied the Genetic Algorithm to fine-tune the models' parameters, which has resulted in significant improvements to the models' accuracy. We have also conducted a comparison between the conventional vector error reduction method and the proposed optimization technique, which has demonstrated that the latter offers reduced computational costs at all levels of the optimization process. We have tested the efficacy of the methods on the actual finite-element-based electromagnetic models of various analog converters, in addition to leveraging the genetic algorithm to optimize the models' accuracy. This comparison revealed that the vector error reduction method in combination with the genetic algorithm can significantly reduce the model's error to below the 0.1% level, which is accompanied by a minimal increase in the computational costs of approximately 50%. Furthermore, the proposed optimization technique has successfully improved the accuracy of the models by at least an order of magnitude compared to the non-optimized vector error reduction methods, which is shown to significantly impact the layout optimization results of the converters. One potential issue with reinforcement learning is that it may not be compatible with fine-grained action spaces. To address this limitation, we propose Coarse-Grained Continuity (CGC), a concept in topological reinforcement learning that ensures optimal policies have continuous policies even when coarse actions are taken. CGC is applied to general Markov decision processes in discrete and continuous settings with transition functions. To demonstrate its power, we establish that a policy with CGC in a certain domain also has CGC in a more general domain. This leads to the discovery of two new properties: weak and strong entropy conditions, which imply the existence of CGC in entropy-maximizing policies. By examining the high-measure CGC entropy condition, we show that only null-measure policies are subject to this property. Finally, we explore open questions and potential applications of CGC in entropy-regularized reinforcement learning. The results were presented at the 34th International Conference on Algorithmic Learning Theory (ATL) in 2022. The CGC framework is now employed to derive properties of optimal policies in a broader context, extending the methodology to derive topological properties of eigenfunctions in Laplacian Spectral Learning in an upcoming publication. A related theoretical verification of the entropy-regularized Q-function (ERQF) property, established in an accompanying paper, is also proposed. From a practical perspective, CGC is utilized to derive properties of optimal policies in a related theoretical verification of the ERQF property, presented at the 29th International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI). The work is expected to facilitate future research on the development of general topological properties of optimal policies in reinforcement learning. In our previous research, we developed a structured representation of animacy where animates were categorized as dynamics with spatial information and inanimates as dynamics without spatial information. This animacy structure is essential in various systems of the human ventral temporal cortex, a region critical for object and animates recognition. Our current research demonstrates that the animacy structure's essence is captured by a small artificial neural network that integrates functional properties, specifically dynamics and spatial components. We found that the interaction between these components and the inanimate and animate groups enabled successful recognition of objects and animates using the ventral temporal cortex's internal representations. Furthermore, the recognition process was found to be bidirectional, where the spatial component recognized objects and the dynamics component recognized animates. These results are substantiated by empirical evidence from various studies. The integration of components and the bidirectionality of the recognition process provide a thorough explanation of the animacy structure's essence in the human ventral temporal cortex. To overcome these issues, a new method of convex optimization-based filter has been developed for use in 2-D and multi-dimensional simulations. This algorithm maintains the original structure of the system at each iteration and has a convergence rate proportional to O(1/k), where k is the iteration number. To evaluate its effectiveness, the new filter has been applied to two different models: a multi-dimensional model for simulating the movement of a contaminant in a system with multiple dimensions and a 2-D model for simulating earthquake surface slip behavior. These tests have demonstrated that the new filter reduces by a significant amount the computational time required to obtain results accurate to a specified level of accuracy, thereby making it feasible to rapidly obtain model states in highly complex situations. To facilitate its use, the source code for this new filter has been made publicly available. Overall, the new convex optimization-based filter has the potential to greatly improve our ability to simulate and analyze complex systems such as those found in oil exploration. A key advantage of this method is its ability to quickly obtain accurate results for a wide range of problems without being affected by computational time complexity issues at high iteration numbers. To validate the effectiveness of the new filter, the method has been tested in multiple simulations. Furthermore, the source code for this new filter has been made publicly available which is expected to significantly contribute to the development of a wide range of efficient simulation algorithms. This could be achieved by substituting traditional time-stepping and spatial resolution methods with the new convex optimization-based filter, thereby maintaining the same level of accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost. We conducted a study to investigate the development of the corona in the black hole candidate MAXI J1535-571 during its 2017-2018 outburst using the Insight-HXMT. Our research involved analyzing quasi-periodic oscillations in the energy spectra and hard X-ray emission patterns. We identified type-C QPOs in the outburst's early stages and observed their spatial distribution using the Insight-HXMT's HEXTE. Our results showed that these QPOs moved from the outer to the inner parts of the accretion disk as the outburst progressed. We observed a correlation between the type-C QPO energy and the disk radius, which supports the fast coronal flow model. Moreover, by mapping the outer boundaries of the corona, we confirmed that the corona extends beyond the outer boundary of the accretion disk. Lastly, our results may imply that the corona in MAXI J1535-571 during its 2017-2018 outburst was disrupted due to a significant mass loss event. However, this finding is currently speculative, and further studies are necessary to validate these conclusions. The Insight-HXMT's high spatial resolution allowed us to obtain more precise measurements of the type-C QPOs and corona properties, which revealed an intriguing link between these phenomena and the accretion disk's structure. In multi-agent reinforcement learning settings with persistent team-based goals,
expectation alignment and coordination among team members is crucial for success.
However, close examination of existing approaches reveals an underserved area:
investigating the psychological aspect necessary for effective coordination.
We introduce transfer empowerment as a representation of the expected level of
agency an agent has in a task and propose a mechanism, the expectational transfer empowerment regulator (ETER), for instilling expectations in agents regarding their teammate's agency level.
Using two games, we evaluate ETER's performance in learning agent collaborations
with limited information available about the agent's capabilities.
The results show ETER's ability to learn cooperative strategies and establish
predictable expectations in a variety of scenarios.
Furthermore, ETER's implementation is straightforward and efficient.
The successful implementation of ETER highlights its potential as a motivating
factor for effective agent collaborations in a variety of scenarios. The source
code for this study is publicly accessible at the following URL:

factor is a promising direction for achieving effective agent collaborations. We
conclude that adapting this mechanism to real-world multi-agent reinforcement learning tasks holds potential for excellent results in terms of performance and reliability. This paper proposes an innovative method to identify objects based on distinct features rather than entire images. The primary advantage of attribute-based methods is their superior performance and efficient multi-class detection capability from a single pass through the data, albeit at the expense of increased memory requirements. Existing attribute-based methods make global comparisons at the expense of efficient multi-class detection. We have developed LoFTR, a local attribute matching detector-free method that employs a transformer-based approach for aligning features. Our experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate that LoFTR performs competitively in comparison to state-of-the-art image-based object detection methods and surpasses state-of-the-art attribute-based methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency. A widely used data-driven approach for converting one-dimensional line features from solar images into vector magnetic field data has a notable bias in its horizontal field component estimates, particularly affecting certain line feature orientations. By examining the underlying physics, we are able to identify the source of this bias as the inherent left-right symmetry of the problem during specific angle ranges. Furthermore, we have developed a simple rectification technique that effectively removes the bias, thereby aligning the results with those from unbiased reconstruction methods. The technique involves adjusting raw field of view data by rotating it by certain angles depending on the orientation and then correcting the values at those rotated positions. By applying this technique, we are able to achieve a notable improvement in accuracy for total field and vector field reconstructions, specifically a 50% reduction in noise for certain scenarios and a 20% reduction in noise for others. The research also points to further improvements being possible with more sophisticated solutions that take into account the full spatial context of magnetic field data. Such advancements could lead to even more precise total and vector magnetic field data at high spatial resolutions, ultimately fostering more accurate research in solar physics. A simple open-source code is provided for other researchers to apply the technique and reproduce our results. The code can be easily accessed at https://github.com/ps210/solar_bias_correction. As the technique is generally applicable to any independent and identically distributed data, we propose its potential use in various other fields as well. In addition to the code, we have also included a supplementary figure showing the more noticeable vector field corrections in a solar image from the HD-SOLFELUX dataset for user reference. The figure can be found at https://doi.org/10.1011/eastj.2021.4156. Figures/7. The higher resolution figure is obtainable at https://zenodo.org/record/3737658. This research focuses on the demand response mechanism of Independent Demand (ID) loads in power networks, developing an energy usage optimization model for home appliances based on energy usage planning and real-time load pricing. The objective of this model is to minimize consumers' energy costs in response to varying real-time load prices and predicted future prices. Initially, energy usage plans for all appliances are created through the use of predicted future load prices and constraints related to the operational periods and energy requirements of each appliance. Subsequently, these energy usage plans are optimized by adjusting the operational schedules of the appliances in response to changing real-time load prices while ensuring compliance with constraints. The study incorporates non-linear and quadratic functions to characterize appliance operations, as well as practical constraints such as minimum and maximum energy limitations for each appliance. These operations are combined in a single mathematical programming problem. The study validates its approach through numerical analysis and compares the outcomes with the results of modern demand response control methods. The ID demand response control method presents an efficient solution for reducing power network load and mitigating voltage problems, even in scenarios involving a large number of consumers and appliances. Additionally, the ID demand response control method offers considerable scope for improving energy costs and operational efficiency when optimized energy usage plans are developed in advance. We have developed a method for identifying metal-deficient stars in the early stages of the Gaia Data Release 3. This involved using a simplified spectral model and training machine learning models on simulated spectra to make robust metallicity predictions. This required addressing two major challenges: leveraging the limited spectral data in Gaia by utilizing a statistically reliable spectral model, and overcoming noise and limitations of the mock spectra generated through model atmospheres and synthetic calculations. We compared our approach with an alternative method involving more complex spectra models, and found that the simpler model produced comparable results. This involved defining a generic stellar type and extracting relevant features from the stellar spectrum. This led to the development of three machine learning models, each based on different sets of spectral features, leading to accurate metallicity predictions within a 0.2 dex margin of error. This allowed us to create an efficient selector for identifying metal-deficient stars at relatively low computational costs. We applied this selector in predicting 25 million star metals from mock observations with 0.05 e- masses of error, which we then compared with the actual metals from DR3 with a agreement of 0.9 dex and a scatter of 0.22. We also looked into the study of RR Lyrae stars, confirming that the metallicity predicted by our models is in line with the most recent literature values. Furthermore, we established that the models we trained are resistant to asteto-photometric transformations, although some bias is introduced with changes in color. This new technique opens the door for utilizing this selector in studying astrophysical phenomena such as horizontal-branch morphology and the metal distribution in the galaxy. It also has applications in planning follow-up observations for low metallicity candidates in surveys like the Extremely Primitive Spectra Survey. We have made the code and tools for this selector available to the public. This research undertakes a comprehensive examination of the fundamental characteristics of morphological complexity in languages, defining it as the interplay of word formation mechanisms and segmental complexity. 

Initial findings reveal that morphological complexity is linked to other forms of linguistic complexity, specifically syntactic and lexical features, yet remains distinct from phonological complexity.

We develop and test a new metric, constructed from observed frequency distributions of words, using datasets from 41 languages to study monomorphic, derived, and compounded forms across various languages.

Results show that languages with higher morphological complexity tend to have increased use of function words in grammar and a broader vocabulary.

Conversely, we found no evidence that compounded words contribute to linguistic complexity in languages of the North European branch, such as Germanic languages, where an alternative strategy of fusion is employed.

On the other hand, we found no correlation between the use of word formation mechanisms and added expression complexity when examining languages of the South European branch, such as Greek and Arabic, where an alternative strategy of inflection is employed. 

Ultimately, we found that morphological complexity is influenced by various factors, including the means by which word parts connect, the part-whole relationship between these factors, the size and versatility of word families, among others, and that such complexity can take many different forms. 

It's also discovered that word formation mechanisms can affect segmental complexity in languages of the North European branch, such as English, but have no effect on the density of word distributions in languages of the South European branch, such as Greek, due to a proven correlation between the size of etymons and morphemic density in languages of the former group. 

In summary, our research defines morphological complexity as involving two distinct aspects - the segmental complexity resulting from word combination and the significant influence of word formation mechanisms on such combination in certain languages. 

It's also concluded that metrics of morphological complexity proposed in prior studies were based on flawed assumptions, and that their correlations with other forms of linguistic complexity were thus artifacts of overlapping factors influencing segmental complexity in general. 

Consequently, our research encourages the examination of the particular conditions of word combination in individual languages rather than assuming universal principles to govern such combination. It's also suggested that inflectional combinations could serve as a baseline for comparing the fundamental properties of monomorphic, derived, and compounded forms across languages. To explore this concept further, a study focused on five galaxy clusters with negligible or positive gravitational lens effects and no satellite galaxies. As a result, it was discovered that the self-interaction cross-section required to explain the missing satellite galaxies in these clusters matches typical values found in literature, but it's essential to examine a broader sample of clusters to confirm this finding. Furthermore, it was suggested that future gravitational lensing observations may serve as an effective tool to detect self-interacting dark matter. Conversely, it was concluded that non-gravitational interactions in dark matter do not adequately explain the observed lens effects in the clusters, and that other mechanisms, such as collisional effects or baryonic activity, could be responsible. To fully understand the implications of these findings, a more comprehensive study incorporating a larger sample of clusters is needed. To connect this theoretical model to observational data, it was applied to a scenario where self-interacting dark matter collapses locally due to gravitational potential variations, resulting in an additional gravitational potential increase. This increased potential can amplify gravitational lens effects in clusters and may serve as an alternative explanation for the observed disparity between strong and weak lens effects. Notably, it was discovered that self-interacting dark matter parameters are consistent with literature values when strong lens effects are present, and that lens effects in clusters can be used to constrain this interaction further, resulting in potential improvements of up to one order of magnitude in such constraints. This process is however challenging and costly as it demands access to entire datasets. To address this limitation, we are exploring a new strategy that allows for learning these essential parameters using only a subset of the data. This is crucial in avoiding data poisoning and leveraging privileged information without revealing it. Our contribution lies in adapting existing model compression techniques for working with incomplete data. We successfully applied these techniques to synthetic subsets, developing novel methods that can utilize compression-efficient fake samples to minimize information disclosure. Using data from Italy and the United States, we have evaluated our approach and revealed that roads with higher traffic volumes and locations with better network connectivity receive more incident reports faster. Through case studies involving road closures and public events in the United States, we have also provided evidence of the accuracy of the identified incidents. To facilitate further research, we have made our data set available for testing and improvement purposes. This paper investigates the performance of a visible, online advertising platform, AdExchange. To maximize revenue from auction participation, bidders must balance two key considerations. Firstly, they need to submit a competitive bid that allows them to win the auction and obtain high revenue. Secondly, they should avoid exceeding their allocated budget, as doing so would preclude participation in future auctions. To address this challenge, we introduce an adaptive bidding strategy, specifically designed for Indian Railways display advertising campaign applications. The proposed method calculates an optimal bid based on the convergence of two critical thresholds, as determined by the user's unique ID and advertising campaign specifics. Moreover, to ensure accuracy, we employed the APB algorithm, incorporating key auxiliary functions and conditions that preserve its original convergence properties. During our evaluation period, this approach achieved a bidding success rate of 70.12% and notably, increased revenue by 189.14% compared to the traditional fixed bidding method. Furthermore, the APB algorithm demonstrated robust performance with growing auction competitiveness and budget constraints. To sum up, our research provides an effective solution for display advertising auction participation, as well as generalizable insights for similar marketing campaigns, including those focused on online display advertising in India and similar rail-based initiatives. We've made our code available on GitHub, specifically in the railway display advertising project. To the best of our knowledge, our research represents an original contribution in this area. The study demonstrates that the curve genus is preserved under a reparameterization that is monotone increasing, assuming the parameter stays within a specific interval. The study further reveals that a particular subset of these curves does not exist in three-dimensional Minkowski space and goes on to classify a certain type of hypersurface curves, or Bertrand curves, in n-dimensional Minkowski space. The study also explores the geometric properties of these curves and provides several illustrative examples. As concerns about biased and manipulative AI techniques grow, researchers are working to develop methods for evaluating and improving the 'interpretability' of algorithms. However, the term remains poorly defined in the literature. This study views interpretability as a facet of the interplay between algorithms and human understanding. Drawing on insights from cognitive science and learning theory, we establish a framework for assessing algorithmic interpretability by considering three key factors: the clarity of the explanatory process, the transparency of the underlying rules, and the ease with which explanations can be gained. Given the subjectivity of these criteria, we develop a systematic approach to measure a second-order concept known as the Cognitive Intricacy Score (CIS) - an quantifiable representation of the complexity of the explanations. By applying this framework to a variety of algorithms, such as tree discriminators and decision trees, we evaluate CIS values and illustrate their usefulness for both identifying areas for improvement in explanatory techniques and comparing the effectiveness of distinct algorithmic explanations in a study involving human subjects. Our research demonstrates that low CIS values enhance human learning, resulting in our proposing the CIS metric as a standardized method for algorithmic interpretability assessments. Furthermore, we show that low CIS values facilitate human understanding, thereby laying the groundwork for a new, human-centered direction in the pursuit of interpretability. The associated code and materials are available for review on https://github.com/DrewRyan/CoreCIS. This repository serves as the primary source for our interpretability methodology, allowing for easy replication of the experiments and data collection processes, thereby promoting public understanding and utilization of the proposed CIS metric. Consequently, future researchers are encouraged to utilize this score to assess a wide variety of explanatory techniques involving human participants, thereby contributing to their development and refinement. The score has also sparked discussions about potential applications in various domains, such as as non-human induced misinformation - or mislead cognition, leading to relevant papers listed in section 7. Ultimately, our research aims to contribute to the further evolution of the field by adopting a more human-centered and cognitive science-informed approach to interpreting algorithmic behavior. The score has since received recognition at a 2022 AAAI paper titled "Human-centered Algorithmic Fairness" as an influential contribution. Extreme events and their significant advancements have garnered extensive attention. 
Statisticians have created two principal extreme value distribution models: 
the parent distribution, directly related to variability, and the frequency 
model, linked to event occurrence. 
While extreme value theory focuses on the former, the theory of extreme values 
in statistics primarily deals with the latter. 
Extremes in various fields, such as weather and extreme sports, are often 
represented by a point process. 
Notably, this representation has several benefits, including being more 
reflective of event patterns and enabling consideration of additional factors 
like spatial distribution and social impact. 
However, this approach has a major shortcoming - it assumes certain non-negative 
values for event intensities, which is not always the case in practice. 
To overcome this limitation, this study proposes a novel method for 
reparameterizing the models and provides an alternative to conventional 
extreme value distribution models for frequency analysis. 
This method is applicable even when negative values are involved and has the 
added advantage of being connected to the standard models through a transformation 
called the Extreme Value Multiplicity Mapping. 
It is notable that this method is connected to standard extreme value distribution 
models only under specific conditions and that such connections are absent when 
negative values are present in extreme data. 
Despite this potential shift in understanding extremes, the method remains 
flexible and allows analysts to interpret results in two ways, including 
standardized testing and location in the parameter space. 
Lastly, this study concludes with considerations on potential applications, 
including connections to frequency analysis and extreme value theory. 
Additionally, researchers are encouraged to explore relationships between 
measurements and patterns through novel approaches, representing a significant 
advance in terms of understanding and analysis. 
This method will enable analysts to look beyond traditional models and 
interpret results in different contexts, including geographical and analytical, 
as well as consider new variables and insights. 
Ultimately, considering this reparameterization could lead to significant 
advances in various scientific and data-driven fields.

This study examines how the particle at the front of the file is dynamically influenced by the particles behind it, using the concept of entropic influences and a semimechanistic approach that takes into account the removal of available entropy. By combining self-consistent method, mean-field approximation, and a perturbation scheme, we derived a decay rate of the self-correlation function of the front particle's position, which increased exponentially with the length of the file. This outcome was further validated by numerical simulations of the continuous-time random-walk model. The distribution also shows that the particle at the front of the file experiences weaker random influences and stronger drift influences as the length of the file increases. This study provides a grounded approach to calculating the exit duration distribution of diffusing particles in single-file motion and offers a framework for understanding entropic influences in thermal mixing systems. Quantum Physics contradicts classical physics' established inference frameworks, specifically Bayesian inference as outlined in Bayes' Theorem, leading to several related issues. This paper offers a comprehensive review of these challenges and demonstrates how quantum applications like quantum learning and scientific inference in quantum settings defy straightforward implementation of Bayes' Theorem. However, we propose that quantum Bayes' Theorem can be effectively applied to such scenarios, and in turn, we derive a convenient method for performing quantum Bayesian inference with general posterior inference targeted. In doing so, we illustrate our approach's value in resolving the puzzle of enhancing entangled spin bit memory, as well as illustrating its potential in quantum physics application through analysis of coin tossing experiments. By examining anentangled memory scenario involving Wigner functions and the quantum extension of Bayes' Theorem, we explore its potential in resolving other related issues, such as the infamous measurement inconsistency problem, including the infamous GHZ paradox in quantum mechanics. By offering possible explanations for these challenges, we demonstrate how quantum Bayes' Theorem can be utilized to resolve these concerns without requiring modification to established quantum mechanics principles. Ultimately, we conclude by discussing potential avenues for further research in theoretical quantum mechanics. Using Gaussian coupled variational method, we initially developed a novel non-perturbative QCD formula for the ground state energy of a system composed of light, scalar particles. This formula effectively incorporates long-range interaction effects between constituents. A series expansion was subsequently derived from this formula in the context of $N+N$ systems, and the resulting QCD term was quantified. It was observed that the QCD contribution to the energy increases as $N$ increases, suggesting a shift from color confinement to chromomagnetic behavior within this domain. A comprehensive examination of various $N+N$ systems, including di-protons, di-lambdas and other spin-isospin configured combinations, was conducted to determine the empirical QCD contribution. These calculations revealed distinct QCD interaction patterns among different $N+N$ systems, characterized by either a focus on kinetic sharing or residual strong forces within the various configurations. A general understanding was thus established on the role of QCD in light hadron compositions. Furthermore, based on these results, we proposed a simple, non-perturbative potential model describing QCD interaction between two color-scalar objects, and the resulting potential spectrum demonstrated agreement with experimental data on a tiny system's mesons. This simple potential also effectively explains the previously calculated and experimental properties of $\Lambda$, including its antiparticle. A potential model grounded in the newly developed QCD formula is expected to produce accurate results not only for tiny systems but also for larger hadrons. A generalization of this simple potential could also lead to novel nuclear force evolution theories, and our developed QCD formula provides essential state energy input for such studies. A comprehensive exploration of the QCD's effect on hadron compositions within the $N+N$ spectrum could lead to significant advancements in our understanding of the strong forces operating at the hadron level. Moreover, our developed QCD formula holds potential as a novel tool for generating potential models that could lead to breakthroughs in the understanding of the strong forces at the hadron level, and its application could offer valuable insights into the role of QCD in tiny hadron systems and beyond. In this research, a novel method for indexing images in dynamic environments has been developed, where objects consist of time-varying sequences of pixels. An algorithm is proposed to efficiently divide motion sequences into distinct sections, where each segment showcases unique objects moving within the frame. These object segments are then grouped based on their spatial distribution, allowing for a hierarchical organization and fast retrieval of motion patterns. A database was created by indexing pixel sequences for various objects under white noise conditions, enabling the effective retrieval of target objects even when severely occluded. Our method demonstrates improved accuracy and efficiency over existing object recognition techniques, especially in scenarios where objects are difficult to identify due to partial concealment or motion blur. This indexing method has practical applications in real-time image analysis, including the tracking and monitoring of objects in security, biomedical, and visual surveillance settings. Additionally, this technique can be applied to aid object grabbing in autonomous robotic systems. Experimental results using synthetic objects under various conditions demonstrate the effectiveness of this indexing method in facilitating fast and accurate object retrieval and grasping.
