Despite both Hermitian and non-Hermitian systems exhibiting topological characteristics, 
a lesser-known concept of correlation-induced topological properties within non-Hermitian systems remains discussed.
A specific one-dimensional non-Hermitian model featuring inter-site correlations has been investigated in this work, 
where interactions enable the transformation of topological edge states into bulk states at low energy.
The research demonstrates how correlation-induced phenomena can influence the topological characteristics of non-Hermitian systems and their implications on their propagating behaviors, 
potentially shedding light on the influence of correlations in non-Hermitian topological systems. 
Furthermore, various extensions of this model are proposed to facilitate flexible control over the correlation-induced effects within non-Hermitian topological systems. 
The discovered properties provide a starting point for the classification and understanding of correlation-induced topological characteristics in non-Hermitian systems and their adaptable applications. 
Lastly, potential experimental realizations of these findings in optical and cold-atom systems are explored, 
denoting a further avenue for the investigation and realization of these novel correlation-induced one-dimensional non-Hermitian topological states. 
The research outcomes present novel perspectives on the topological characteristics of non-Hermitian systems and their adaptation in their design and manipulation. 
An additional bonus for the quantum community lies in the proposed feasible realization in both cold-atom and optical-lattice setups. 
The existing topological non-Hermitian systems are largely based on the replacement of Hermitian Haldane model with their non-Hermitian counterparts, 
wherein the influence of correlations on these systems has not been explored until now, 
whereas the model in this study reveals a unique context where correlations alone induce topological characteristics in a non-Hermitian system. 
Therefore, the research has fundamental significance in understanding the nature and behavior of topological non-Hermitian systems and their generalization. 
The possibility of achieving topological edge states with negative correlations also opens up novel avenues for the design and manipulation of non-Hermitian topological systems.

Previous research suggests that consistency in speech characteristics conveys social traits such as warmth and competence. We aimed to infuse synthetic speech with distinct social attributes by manipulating speaker consistency, and explored the effect of consistency on perceived traits and familiarity. We varied the consistency of articulation, speech rate, and voice quality in English text-to-speech production and conducted a listening study. Participants indeed identified higher consistency with the traits as warm and competent, yet they couldn't consistently associate the traits with specific levels of consistency. Furthermore, increasing consistency didn't significantly affect perceived familiarity. These results align with prior studies and underline the importance of speaker consistency in conveying social characteristics through synthetic speech. In light of recent neutrino data, particularly the nearly determined light neutrino mass ordering and a future expected mass gap, a minimal theoretical framework is examined. This framework incorporates a modular A4 symmetry, utilizing the sixth power of the modular parameter, and its interaction with gauged U(1)_(B-L) flavor symmetry. To address the issue of a flavor-dependent quark mass matrix and correctly identify the experimentally established pattern of light quarks, an extended scalar sector is introduced with multiple sets of scalar fields, ensuring invariance under both modular and gauged U(1)_(B-L) symmetries. Gauged symmetry generates seesaw-type models for relating neutrino masses to the assumed dark matter candidate, here a charged fermion L. When this charged dark matter experiences standard model interactions, its lifetime is determined, yielding results consistent with the current lower experimental bounds on the dark matter lifetime from the mediators of the standard model and the Z' boson. Furthermore, the model's predicted behavior of dark matter is similar to that of ref. [Heckler, arXiv:1706.0518], especially in terms of the number of relativistically decoupled dark matter particles and their mass dependence on the assumed dark matter parameter k. In addition to dark matter to the standard model particles interaction, we also find evidence of non-standard model physics, specifically non-universal Z' boson coupling and CP violation within the charged lepton sector. We examine two main examples of properly lowering the light neutrino mass, namely the contribution of the neutrino L to the standard model and the light neutrino mass via the mediators of the standard model and the Z' boson. Example 1, with k much less than Lambda_QCD, relies on non-standard model physics, while generating correctly the experimentally established pattern of light quarks. Example 2, with k approximately equal to the Fermi momentum of dark matter, relies on universal Z' boson coupling and correctly identifies the experimentally established pattern of light quarks. Object detection and classification in real-world scenarios are hindered by changes in background settings. Therefore, it is crucial to identify and isolate areas of interest within images before processing them further. This task can be efficiently achieved through the application of alteration detection methods. Two such methods, Deep Convolutional Autoencoders (DCAs), play a vital role in this process. In this paper, we explore a two-stage approach to alteration detection, using DCAs. Stage one involves using a primary DCA to capture a broad range of features in an image. Stage two utilizes a secondary DCA to extract detailed spatial patterns in an image. These patterns are then measured against features extracted in step one to identify and mark altered regions. This combined approach, grounded in the principles of unsupervised learning and deep neural networks, demonstrates exceptional efficacy on the VSI dataset, outperforming existing alteration detection methods by incorporating transfer learning, leveraging a larger set of features, and fine-tuning DCA architectures to emphasize spatial information in addition to visual features. Moreover, it's notable that the secondary DCA's ability to identify altered regions surpasses that of a supervised object detection network, highlight the efficacy of unsupervised learning in altering region detection. Our code is publicly available on GitHub. Experimental results show that the combination of secondary DCA's detected altered regions with the fast R-CNN network results in a significant 4.6% improvement in precision and 2.7% improvement in recall, bringing the overall performance close to being indistinguishable from ground truth. This study showcases the effectiveness of the proposed two-stage approach, its implementation details, and the importance of unsupervised feature learning in alteration detection. Moreover, it suggests future alteration detection methods seek to integrate transfer learning, improve feature set designs, and refine DCA architectures to optimize performance. Following the publication of this work, the proposed method has been tested on various other datasets and the code has been used as a baseline in a related research paper titled 'Deep Learning Techniques for Alteration Detection and Object Localization in Hyperspectral Images' published by A. A. S. Y. Khalifa in 2020 at the SPIE 2577, Imaging Spectroscopy XVII conference. Recently, the proposed method has received an award from the data fusion school organized by the Data Fusion School program in July 2020. The code also received an award from the Asian conference on perceptive computing & virtual engineering at the IIE 2020 conference. The code related to this work is publicly available on

A well-established, research-oriented approach called $\Lambda$CDM is the basis for the Standard Model in Cosmology. Researchers have developed an enhanced version of this model, incorporating a modified cycle pattern instead of the conventional dark energy scenario. The new EEC cyclical cosmology suggests that the universe underwent an eternal cycle of expansion and contraction. By applying cyclic principles, the universe's evolution can be extended beyond the conventional $\Lambda$CDM model and new predictions made regarding EEC universe properties can be generated. The study includes an estimation of the present-day value of the Hubble constant, suggests a possible explanation for the missing dark matter in galaxy centers, and provides evidence that cosmic strings may have contributed to the formation of galaxies. A thorough investigation into dark energy and dark matter candidates that could play a crucial role in EEC cyclical models is also presented. Analysis into unusual optical effects caused by cosmic cyclicity is documented, and the possibilities of detecting EEC signatures in near future astronomical observations are explored. The study aims to stimulate further research into the cyclical behavior of our Cosmos and enhance our understanding of the universe's evolution from the earliest possible time to its current state. Additional theoretical components to EEC models are also presented, including the postulation of an existing cycle before the Big Bang and investigation into the possibilities of reverse cycling, where the universe expands instead of contracts. The study is primarily based on the latest research published in 2020-2022 on EEC models and is organized into distinct sections, with each chapter building on the last, allowing readers to follow the narrative from start to finish. A comprehensive bibliography of 121 relevant papers is also included, offering readers who wish to delve deeper into specific topics and studies listed in the bibliography (for those who wish to pursue further research). A total of seven distinct chapters are presented, exploring various aspects of EEC models and their impact on their behavior and properties, including behavior on different scales, possible dark energy and dark matter candidates, and the study of optical effects caused by cosmic cyclicity. In addition to standard chapters, two special chapters are also presented, focusing on the possible detection of gravitational waves in the context of EEC models, and the study of the possible impact of cyclical behavior on the development of modern quantum theories and the very early universe and the first laws of physics that governed the development and evolution of the universe. The study concludes, and our understanding of the universe, including its behavior and properties, may need to be revised or corrected, and the study serves as an inspiration

Recent studies suggest that quantum mechanics' predictions might surpass expectations within the realm of cosmology, however a theoretical barrier exists limiting its integration with reality - the requirement for temporal coherence. In response, a new theory known as the Invariant-set hypothesis has been proposed, postulating the existence of an ever-changing set of hidden variables to address this limitation. We explore this concept by examining its potential application to a fundamental process in our universe, the pair production of photons, and compare its efficacy to that of a superdeterministic approach. We further seek to identify similarities and differences between these theories, particularly in how they can be applied to a hidden-variable model. Our model employs a strict deterministic framework, which we have refined to accurately reflect the pair production process. We have also developed a precise formula detailing the amount of coherence required for this process, providing a clear benchmark for the Invariant-set hypothesis and superdeterministic approaches. We have calculated the coherence requirement for the Invariant-set hypothesis and found it to be significantly higher than that of the superdeterministic approach, by several orders of magnitude. While the Invariant-set hypothesis demonstrates the potential to replicate quantum mechanics' predictions for the pair production process, it appears that the superdeterministic approach is significantly more effective, making it a stronger candidate for explaining cosmological data. Our research confirms that the Invariant-set hypothesis and superdeterministic approaches have distinct characteristics, with the former relying on an intricate web of hidden variables to replicate the pair production process, whereas the superdeterministic approach can achieve the same result with much simpler means, by fine-tuning its free parameters. We have also established a new coherence requirement formula, providing a clear and standardized metric for these types of theories. By refining this metric, we have further highlighted the significant coherence requirement needed to replicate the pair production process in the Invariant-set hypothesis framework. Our calculation shows that the amount of coherence required exceeds the overall energy of our universe, by several orders of magnitude, indicating that the Invariant-set hypothesis is largely inadequate as a theoretical framework. Our research concludes with suggestions for potential modifications to the Invariant-set hypothesis to make it more viable as a theoretical explanation for the pair production process. One such revision could involve incorporating a fine-tuned 'quantum radiation factor' to regulate the amount of coherence required to replicate the pair production process, by linking it to the total energy of our universe. By incorporating this modification, we have verified that the superdeterministic approach remains significantly more effective than the Invariant-set hypothesis.

Precise data retrieval depends on effective metadata, and keyphrases play a crucial role in this process, enabling users to filter and limit search queries to specific topics, thus reducing storage consumption and query complexity for real-time search solutions. We analyze how Neural Network (NN) based keyphrase detection systems perform under resource-constrained settings of IoT devices, given that NNs are increasingly being used for keyphrase extraction in various applications. To address this issue, we evaluate the computational and memory demands of four NN architectures - CNN, CNN-LSTM, LSTM, and Transformer - and assess their accuracy on a dataset of 1,000 books using the standard metrics, F-score and ROUGE score. Our experimental outcome indicates that NN models can efficiently generate keyphrases for short texts, but their performance deteriorates for longer texts due to their inherent characteristics. To overcome this limitation, we propose a text segmentation approach that splits keyphrases into optimal language chunks to ensure accurate and efficient keyphrase extraction. Our results show that F-score and ROUGE score can reach up to 0.80 and 0.83 for a single NN model, and even higher values can be attained through combining the predictions of multiple NN architectures with the proposed segmentation strategy, thus providing a practical solution for keyphrase detection under the constraints of IoT devices. Additionally, the proposed keyphrase detection system exhibits fast inference times, processing a 1 million search queries per minute, and its code is publicly available at GitHub. Overall, the contribution of this research lies in assessing the capabilities of NN architectures for keyphrase detection and developing a simple yet efficient text segmentation approach to apply these models to real-world applications under the constraints of IoT devices. Finally, NN-based keyphrase detection has several potential use cases in the fields of Information Retrieval and Natural Language Processing, and its public demonstration can be accessed at GitHub. Furthermore, the paper provides a comprehensive overview of related work in the area of keyphrase extraction, and it contributes to the advancement of IoT-related research by exploring the capabilities of NN architectures for keyphrase detection. Moreover, the proposed search engine architecture can serve as a starting point or reference for various NN-based keyphrase extraction models, and its public demonstration can be accessed at GitHub. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first comprehensive assessment of NN architectures for keyphrase detection and a simple yet efficient text segmentation approach to apply these models to keyphrase extraction under the constraints of IoT devices. The widespread use of real-time operating systems in embedded devices has facilitated their programming, making it easier to develop and manage real-time applications. Hypervisors, acting as virtual machines, manage hardware resources and provide a sandboxed environment for guest operating systems to execute safely. In embedded systems with resource constraints, the virtualization overhead can be a significant concern, compelling the implementation of custom hypervisors to strike a balance between security and performance. Given the mixed importance of modern embedded systems, this research introduces T-Visor, a hypervisor designed for embedded real-time systems and capable of supporting hard real-time applications. Furthermore, it includes hardware virtualization assistance in its execution, making it suitable for missions that require high reliability. A case study was conducted, comparing the performance of T-Visor, Xen, and Windows, demonstrating that T-Visor results in the shortest creation time and is close to the performance of Windows. Moreover, its creation time is significantly less than Xen. A practical experiment was also performed to verify the correctness of T-Visor, indicating that it can effectively support hard real-time applications. In terms of its virtualization overhead, the results show that T-Visor achieves low creation time and is capable of effectively managing embedded real-time systems. The source code of T-Visor is available for researchers and developers to utilize. In summary, this research presents a new concept, mixed importance embedded real-time systems, and introduces T-Visor as a hypervisor for mixed importance embedded real-time systems with hardware virtualization assistance. A practical experiment was also performed, verifying the effectiveness and feasibility of T-Visor in supporting hard real-time applications. However, addressing 360-degree stitching poses unique challenges due to the rotational symmetry of panoramic images, which makes object location and orientation particularly difficult. We enhance the 2018 Panoramic Stitching approach by incorporating gravitational prior into feature matching, thereby making object rotation in 3D space a well-defined problem. We also propose a novel gravitational prior that outperforms previous methods and achieves more accurate results with fewer feature matches. Experiments show that using MA-based frameworks with our proposed gravitational prior results in better performance on both synthetic and real-world datasets compared to traditional and DeepNavi approaches. We release our code on GitHub for public use. We also conduct a comprehensive analysis of current Panoramic Stitching approaches, comparing their performance based on specific evaluation metrics in a detailed classification. We also make a series of refinement enhancements to our initial code, addressing common problems such as MA-based underconfidence, image distortion, and artifact elimination. When two groups of oscillators with synchronized frequencies, each having its own phase, are coupled, a new type of synchronization occurs. Research has shown that such systems can experience stable, synchronized chimeras even with strong internal connections within each group. However, but a new study has found that when both groups have identical oscillators and uniform connections within them, a new type of synchronization occurs. It has been found that in this case, complete synchronization of the two groups is not stable and that chimeras do occur, but are dependent on various parameters, such as the strength of the couplings and the frequencies of the oscillators. Interestingly, it has also been found that in this case, small changes to these parameters can cause systems that were previously in a chimeras state to switch to a completely synchronized state. This new type of behavior has not been previously observed in these types of systems and involves a switch from one chimeras state to another. The study has also considered systems where the frequencies of the oscillators are naturally random, rather than being fixed, and has found that in this case, more complex behaviors occur, with the emergence of multiple chimeras states and a non-partnership dynamic. It has also been considered in this case, how the behavior of these types of systems can be changed by various types of frequency distributions. Controller learning has become a preferred approach for developing complex system controllers without extensive human expertise. However, controllers created using this method often fail to adapt and maintain their effectiveness in real-world systems with unforeseen issues. To address this limitation, this research develops a new method for designing controllers that can handle errors and ensure system continuity. By integrating probabilistic model uncertainty into reinforcement learning, the proposed method achieves controller resilience through enhanced adaptability and error correction. To demonstrate its effectiveness, the method was tested on a nuclear reactor example, showcasing its ability to find controllers capable of recovering from unexpected events and maintaining safe operation. Overall, this research successfully integrates controller learning and model uncertainty to achieve continued system functionality in the presence of unexpected problems. To support this, a comprehensive Python package is provided, including both model-based and model-free implementations of the method, as well as detailed example demos to facilitate reproduction and expansion of the method for various applications. The package can be accessed at https://cassis-git.github.io/resilient_controller/search_code. The code is also available for viewing. A thorough evaluation of the method is performed, examining its ability to find controllers under different scenarios and assessing its dependence on model quality. Additionally, a comparison of the method to existing controller reinforcement learning techniques is conducted, verifying its capacity for error recovery and system continuity. Finally, some considerations for the practical application of the method are discussed, including potential challenges and obstacles. The impact of the method is summarized, providing a concise overview of its innovations and contributions to the literature in controller learning and system resilience. The presentation concludes by highlighting promising research directions inspired by the method, including the exploration of additional approaches for ensuring system continuity in the presence of unexpected problems. The related impact is summarized in appendix C and D, specifically in the vision statement and impact statement of CASISi. The data collected during experiments is documented in the experimental results section in the search code repository. The method's potential applications and generalizations are discussed in the appendix as well as the search code repository. To facilitate adoption of the method, a detailed guide on how to use it for similar scenarios is provided in appendix as well as the search code repository. In various fields, mechanisms driving pattern formation are highly debated and
often misunderstood. As the simple framework of reaction-diffusion equations has
failed to fully explain observed patterns, researchers have incorporated user-defined
parameters. However, this approach raises significant epistemological concerns,
as it blurs the line between explanatory and descriptive mechanisms. We address
this concern by leveraging results from stochastic dynamics and path integral
formalism. Firstly, we illustrate the benefits of considering marooned particles
in homogeneous environments. Secondly, we extend our findings to more complex
heterogeneous settings, yielding novel, hereditable correlation functions.
Using this general formalism, we recreate the Marangoni effect within a fluid,
and examine the emergence of spatial patterns arising from the synthesis of
polymers. Through this combination of novel concepts and rigorous mathematical
approach, we clarify the pattern-formation process, avoiding the necessity of
introducing ad-hoc parameters. Instead, we identify an exclusive option: either
the pattern-forming dynamics is autonomous and self-sustaining, or it is an
organic extension of hereditable information endogenous to the system under
consideration. This assessment offers a crucial framework for evaluating and
unraveling the underlying mechanisms driving pattern formation. As a result, we
obtain a clearer understanding of the emergence of patterns, now free from the
influence of external, artificially introduced elements. Furthermore, we have
established a method for characterizing pattern-forming dynamics using
experimentally accessible measures, even in cases where spatial patterns may not
arise. Finally, we have identified a fundamental distinction between systems
featuring hereditable information and those supported solely by external factors. 
This theory has far-reaching implications, potentially reshaping various areas of
research, from biology to chemistry and geology. To demonstrate its applicability
in these fields, we have applied our theory to four prominent examples, 
temporally structured organisms, cholesteric liquid crystals, black smokers, and 
earth's geologic layers. By embracing this new pattern-forming paradigm, 
researchers may now design and explore novel materials, uncover hidden
complications, and recognize key underlying factors. Additionally, this theory has
significant consequences for our understanding of the origins of life on Earth and
potentially other planets. We contend that life may emerge as an organic
extension of hereditable information, endogenous to various Earth systems.

The deflection of light by gravity was first described by Georg Birkhoff in 1932 as an outcome resulting from the combination of two factors - the inherent curvature of spacetime and the effect of isolated mass. My previous research revealed that the latter factor, termed gravitational holonomy, contributes a component distinct from curvature. This paper presents a thorough, group-theoretic explanation of gravitational holonomy, incorporating a novel version of Birkhoff's formula for light deflection that encompasses both curvature and holonomy effects. Additionally, this framework serves as the foundational structure for a novel theory of gravity, encompassing both general relativity and the Pons-Davies-Rudolph (PDR) solution as specific cases. By comparing the predictions of the PDR solution and the Einstein theory of general relativity, our analysis demonstrates a consistent agreement between the PDR solution and the measured form factor in observations of 100 radio quasars by Weeks et al. We also provide an explanation for why the PDR solution does not exhibit an inverse square law dependence on mass. Finally, this framework, having been rooted in the fundamental principles of Lorentz transformation and tensor analysis, is a comprehensive and rigorous mathematical treatise on the concept of gravitational holonomy. It does not rely on any form of Wheeler's geodesic deviation or geometric optics approximation as in the work by Pons et al. or RD, as both of their approaches only provided intuitive insights and not a rigorous mathematical explanation of gravitational holonomy. This treatise is a milestone in the ongoing debate between the Einstein's general theory of relativity and the new physical findings from the PDR solution of Einstein's field equations. We note that the PDR solution is not in contradiction with any other findings as it is often alleged but rather offers a simple and complete resolution to various on-going disputes in the field. We hope that our analysis will serve as an inspiration for future research in the field of study. We would also like to point out a possible future direction for theoretical physics that is consistent with our analysis. This is the possibility of developing what we propose for a new version of classical gravity that is consistent with general relativity, to a new version of quantum gravity that is consistent with both the PDR solution and the established quantum gravitational theories. We propose that our analysis here and in the past offers a complete and consistent view of both classical and quantum gravitational theories. Our work involves characterizing these sequences in terms of partition trees and determining formulas for the number of such sequences according to their maximum hook length. Additionally, we offer conjectures related to sequences of hook lengths associated with odd parity Young diagrams. These results lead to new enumerations among Dyck paths and alternating lattice paths. Finally, we obtain asymptotic expressions for the sums of hook lengths in these multiplicative sequences. The evidence suggests that our conjectures hold true. The study has implications for Young scholars, leading to some interesting observations. The work begins by exploring the sequences of hook lengths one and three, which involves Young diagrams and alternating lattice paths. Subsequently, the focus shifts to sequences of hook lengths two and three, encompassing odd parity Young diagrams and alternating non-dominant lattice paths. Notably, the bulk of the sequences of hook lengths two and three corresponds to Young diagrams with five or fewer rows, while the sequences of hook lengths one and three are confined to three or fewer rows. Our analysis is facilitated by the utilization of partition trees, enabling us to present comprehensive generating functions for these sequences. The enumeration of sequences of hook lengths two and three is extended to those associated with set partitions, satisfying specific conditions as per the work of Gao-Moriah-Walecki and Han-Ramirez. The other sequences of hook lengths two and three can be obtained through iterations of this length-two sequence, effectively making them first-order. We utilize the concept of free homogeneous sums to further explore these sequences of hook lengths. Quantum mechanics predicts that particles may traverse the Schr\"{o}dinger "wall" at the point of classically inaccessibility under certain conditions. Researchers have created an experimental approach that allows for the direct measurement of this phenomenon, known as quantum tunneling. Unlike previous studies focusing on particle tunneling through a potential barrier, our experiment examines tunneling in a system with an indeterminate spin, which introduces unpredictable disturbances during the measurement process. By utilizing the spin-Higgs invariant Larmor clock as a model system and linking the measured time delays to the free particle model, our results demonstrate that these time delays can be entirely attributed to the particle's quantum tunneling motion. We found the tunneling duration exhibits an exponential relationship with the reciprocal square root of the time dilation factor. The value of the exponential coefficient was found to be approximately 0.9576, matching theoretical expectations. Furthermore, our experiment confirms that even minor spin disturbances may cause substantial time delays, challenging classical notions of time. The experiment's findings also highlight the inherent connection between quantum mechanics and relativity, showing that space-time irregularities may be detectable through direct measurement. The experiment's data may also contribute to an understanding of the underlying irregularities in space-time. Potential applications of this experiment's findings could lead to the development of new quantum clocks capable of operating independently of Earth's rotation and positioning in space. Moreover, tuning the experiment's conditions may enable the direct observation of quantum tunneling in systems with effectively infinite mass, effectively rendering the experiment's concept novel and groundbreaking. The experiment's data provides strong empirical evidence for the existence of quantum tunneling, providing a more in-depth and intricate understanding of the phenomenon. The experiment's success may serve as a model for future studies on quantum mechanics and gravitational physics, potentially leading to significant breakthroughs in the field. The experiment's data could also be applied to ongoing discussions surrounding modifications to the quantum tunneling effect, particularly those proposed in the context of the quantum gravitational "foam" model. The experiment's findings could also shed new light on possible quantum effects in the environment surrounding planets, potentially offering a novel explanation for the phenomenon of "tempus perduus" - a type of temporal irregularity. The experiment's data could also be employed in calculations estimating the magnitude of temporal irregularities resulting from planet gravitational interactions, offering a fresh perspective on the subject. The experiment's success may potentially lead to a more elaborate and attribute-rich model of quantum gravitational "foam," effectively classifying the phenomenon as both quantum and relativistic

Subsequently, we apply the dominant twist expansion to the eigenvalues of this energy matrix and determine the expression for the twist distribution profiles of P-wave mesons, where the profiles are contingent upon the spin and relative spin-orbit coupling parameters involved. Ultimately, we present our findings in a format that enables comparison with relativistic theory, where we observe increasing agreement between the two theories as the spin-orbit coupling strength is amplified. As the spin-orbit coupling strength approaches infinity, the P-wave results we have obtained fully align with their relativistic counterparts, where the dominant twist distribution profiles exhibit odd-order peaks in twist $\tau = 2$. Similar peak patterns can also be observed on the negative twist side of these distributions. Our analysis further reveals that the shapes of these dominant twist distribution profiles naturally evolve from a Gaussian distribution for weak spin-orbit coupling to more distorted forms as the spin-orbit coupling strength is increased. By increasing the spin $s$ from 0 to 1, we notice a symmetry breakdown in the twist distribution profiles for $s = 1$, where the distorted forms exhibit asymmetry. Three distinct concepts are introduced: a novel shape theory, a corresponding metric structure, and a particular solution to the Ricci-flat equation. This is accomplished by extending existing measures of geometric significance, such as Hausdorff and log-Hausdorff Gromov widths, to broader categories. Furthermore, the study examines the properties and examples of shapes associated with riemannian manifolds, exploring their connections with group shapes and CAT(0) cone structures. It is demonstrated that shapes are closely related to a particular class of Ricci-flat metrics, which in turn have implications for the study of harmonic maps and the stability of hyperk\"ahler manifolds. By establishing this connection, the research resolves a longstanding question regarding the existence of Ricci-flat left-invariant metrics on free groups. The work also includes a comprehensive study on the relationship between the shapes of riemannian manifolds and their CAT(0) properties. Lastly, the research contributes to our understanding of the geometric significance of free groups through the investigation of the existence of Ricci-flat left-invariant metrics. Specifically, it is proven that any non-trivial free group can be endowed with a left-invariant Ricci-flat metric if and only if it has the CAT(0) property, thereby answering a decades-old conjecture. As a direct result, the research provides a negative answer to a question regarding the existence of harmonic maps from certain manifolds to hyperk\"ahler manifolds, especially when the base space is a nilmanifold with the CAT(0) property. The study also establishes a strong connection between the geometric significance of free groups and the stability of hyperk\"ahler manifolds, where it is shown that a particular class of harmonic maps stably exist from certain nilmanifolds to a class of hyperk\"ahler manifolds with the truncated hyperk\"ahler metric. The work is completed by demonstrating that, contrary to expectations, the geometric significance of free groups is far from being a direct consequence of their algebraic properties. By constructing an explicit example, the research proves that a non-trivial property associated with certain classes of free groups is preserved under a particular type of algebraic and group-theoretic operation. Furthermore, the study reveals that the property in question is unrelated to the most algebraically extreme form of group operations. Consequently, the research raises a series of challenging problems regarding the relationships between various distinct concepts of geometric significance, shapes, and group operations. This study establishes a connection between permutation functions over finite fields with order divisible by 3 and multivariate polynomial functions through permutation vectors, and introduces complete permutation functions over finite fields with order divisible by 3, extending the concept of complete permutation polynomials to higher dimensions. Several examples of such complete permutation functions and their associated automorphism groups are presented, and the feasibility of utilizing complete permutation functions to build APN functions is evaluated. The study demonstrates that no such complete permutation functions exist over finite fields with order divisible by 3 and degree 3, and presents a constructive method for mapping affine permutation functions over finite fields with order divisible by 3 to complete permutation functions. The relationship between permutation functions over finite fields with order divisible by 3 and colored and multicolored Sidon sums is also explored, and several instances of such complete permutation functions are identified. The study concludes with the presentation of examples of complete permutation functions that induce regular 3-cycles when mapped to the field through the derivative, and of complete permutation functions that are invariant under the Frobenius map. These examples reinforce the concept that, in the majority of cases, degree 3 is a threshold that has been difficult to cross in the realm of permutation functions over finite fields with order divisible by 3. It is also noted that, unlike permutation polynomials, permutation functions do not form an algebraic structure and therefore cannot be induced by automorphisms of the field. Human intestinal parasitic infections cause significant issues in most parts of the world, leading to discomfort, malnutrition and even life-threatening situations in severe cases. However, identifying these parasites typically involves time-consuming and labor-intensive processes for patients. With the advancement of digital technology and image processing techniques, studies have been conducted to develop automated methods for classifying intestinal parasites using microscopical images. This research applies a Categorical Deep Belief Network approach to C. lymphaticeri, T. spiralis, H. nana and E. vermicularis images, using a dataset of 3000 categorized specimens collected from various sources. Results indicate that CDB achieves an accuracy of 88.95%, surpassing alternative models such as Convolutional Neural Networks, Lateral Distribution Networks and Recurrent Neural Networks, which demonstrate lower accuracy rates. Importantly, CDB's approach enables efficient classification of intestinal parasites with minimal computational requirements. This research utilizes a dataset of images publicly accessible at https://doi.org/10.6084/M1.v1.464535. This method may have practical applications in clinical settings, though patient specimens may require pre-processing due to various distortions, indicating a need for further study. Nonetheless, CDB demonstrates promising results and could potentially excel in tasks beyond parasite categorization, such as regression and clustering operations. Furthermore, its capabilities in data analysis make it a suitable candidate for operations in restricted areas with limited infrastructure. In summary, this study effectively combines computer vision techniques with a deep learning approach to tackle a significant challenge in public health and medical fields. In addition to its practical contributions, it also expands the existing body of research in these areas. To achieve agile flight maneuvers, fixed-wing micro aeronautics faces the challenge of maintaining stability between flight phases. This problem can be solved by optimizing control coefficients in a Plane in a Angle (PIA) controller, leading to the development of PIA controllers. However, the process of finding suitable PIA coefficients through simulation is time-consuming and demands a high level of computational power. Consequently, the authors propose an efficient method to determine PIA coefficients, referred to as Protocol for Interacting and Dynamic adaptation of Angels (PIDA), utilizing a unique genetic filter in conjunction with the Dual Simplex Algorithm. This approach is able to rapidly converge to optimal coefficients, even at low computational costs, thereby accelerating the process of implementing agile flight capabilities on fixed-wing micro aeronautics vehicles. Fuzzy sets are employed to adaptively fine-tune the search space, ensuring that the obtained coefficients remain within realistic pilot control capabilities. Consequently, the combination of this genetic filter and Dual Simplex Algorithm enables the rapid identification of optimal PIA coefficients for executing agile flight maneuvers. Furthermore, the presence of a accurate aerodynamic model is not a prerequisite for the implementation of PIDA, as the Stochastic Dual Simplex Algorithm is capable of generating suitable control coefficients even with approximate model representations. The efficacy of the proposed PIDA approach is demonstrated through its successful application in enabling stable and agile flight maneuvers of a quasi-quadrotor system and a real vehicle. The results illustrate the remarkable capacity of PIDA to attain steady and fluent flight in the most demanding flight scenarios, thereby establishing its significant potential in the field of research on agile flight and micro aeronautics. The proposed method is universally applicable to any fixed-wing aircraft equipped with a flight simulator or model of aerodynamic dynamics. This study presents the related code in MatLab and provides detailed instructions for reproducing its results, thereby ensuring high levels of practical implementation. Consequently, the implementation of PIDA represents an highly efficient computational method capable of bringing agile fixed-wing micro aeronautics vehicles to life. This expression matches the pion-nucleon scattering data to a level of precision comparable to that achieved by the most recent partial wave analyses. It is demonstrated how altering the two parameters could influence low-energy pion-nucleon potentials, thereby affecting quantities like the pion-nucleon sigma term and the mass of the sigma meson. Furthermore, the developed expression is expanded to account for additional components in the pion-nucleon S-matrix, considering possible contributions from the cut states, a hairpin contribution, and an effective field theory description. Finally, the implications of the established expression are discussed in the context of chiral effective field theory and the pion loop correction. The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) employs a complex system for identifying and measuring particle collisions. As the CMS detector undergoes upgrades for the High-Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC) project, it will experience increased rates of particle collisions. In preparation, the CMS collaboration conducted a study to evaluate the performance of the CMS detector's phase-1 pixel pilot system during actual particle collisions at the LHC. Specifically, the research focused on the detector's edge reconstruction performance in the vicinity of the trigger threshold. Through this analysis, the CMS collaboration demonstrated that the detector is capable of accurately identifying particle collisions above this threshold with high precision. In this study, the CMS collaboration utilized the equivalent of approximately 6.2 femtometers in terms of single-hit resolution along the measurement plane for the pixel pilot layers. Since this single-hit resolution affects the measurement of the particle's edge position, the CMS collaboration developed a novel method for determining the position uncertainty at the edge. Notably, the bulk reconstruction pilot does not contribute to this positive outcome. In addition, the CMS collaboration found that implementing a more stringent criterion for selecting pilot hits does not enhance the edge reconstruction performance. Moreover, the edge reconstruction performance exhibits independence from the intensity of the particle collisions. Based on these positive outcomes, the CMS collaboration is confident that it can achieve the desired objective of the HL-LHC project. In support of this goal, the CMS collaboration will undertake a thorough analysis to fine-tune its simulation models for use in future physics analyses. As part of this effort, the CMS collaboration will carry out a detailed investigation to establish whether the bulk reconstruction pilot contributes to the bulk measurement of the particle's position. In addition, the CMS collaboration will have to optimize the criteria used for selecting pilot hits in order to achieve the desired goal. In terms of the detector itself, the CMS collaboration will utilize the results of this study to refine its parameterization model for incorporating the detector's edge reconstruction performance into its simulation models for high-intensity particle collisions. These parameterization models will be essential in determining the suitability of the detector's output for specific scientific applications at the HL-LHC. In conclusion, the CMS collaboration is preparing to undertake a comprehensive analysis to establish the desired detector performance for the HL-LHC project. As part of this effort, the CMS collaboration will engage in a thorough theoretical investigation to establish use of the detector's trigger threshold for selecting pilot hits in its simulation models for high-intensity particle collisions. To assess the reliability of predictive machine learning models, we developed a practical evaluation framework that goes beyond conventional metrics like accuracy and loss functions. This comprehensive tool enables users to evaluate how robust their models are in the face of synthetic data manipulations. This approach allows for deeper model diagnosis by identifying which features are most affected by classification errors and how these errors correlate across related classification tasks. To showcase the effectiveness of our evaluation framework, we employed it on a FinLit dataset from the Data Science Bowl competition. Our results reveal that classification models are particularly susceptible to manipulations involving the most influential features, which often receive the most attention during data collection. Furthermore, we discovered strong links between our evaluation results and the performance of classification models, indicating that our evaluation framework can aid in model optimization. To facilitate accessible model evaluation, we developed the ScEval library, which simplifies the implementation of our evaluation framework for anyone to use. This library combines the advantages of interactive exploration with high-performance evaluation, making it easy to evaluate a wide range of models on various synthetic manipulations. Through our application on the FinLit dataset, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our evaluation framework and provide practical insights for developers to create more robust classification models in practice. Finally, we believe that our evaluation framework has the potential to contribute to ongoing discussions around model explainability, fairness, and transparency by offering a practical way to identify and address potential weaknesses in classification models. Using Quantum Computing Learning (QCL), a novel method has been developed to identify patterns in vast datasets by combining quantum computing and machine learning. This method has been bolstered with an advanced error correction technique, specifically tailored for (5,4) quantum codes, as detailed in a recently published study. To assess the efficacy of this approach, researchers have been employing SQUID - a widely regarded, open-source quantum computing framework. Our research presents a comprehensive overview of QCL, implemented on a quantum simulator with support for noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices. By employing QCL, a quantum-based classifier can be created directly from a binary dataset, without needing an initial classical model. This pattern recognition capability is derived from repeatedly measuring data samples, which are then used to generate a quantum circuit through QCL's pattern learning. Subsequently, the resulting quantum circuit can be employed to predict the classification of new, unseen data. To demonstrate QCL's advantages, our study included comparisons with a classical baseline classifier, revealing superior resilience and performance with the inclusion of error correction. Furthermore, simulations on NISQ devices showed that the noise threshold required to deactivate QCL was significantly higher (0.42) in comparison to classical methods. Our study showcases the potential for QCL to be executed efficiently on near-term quantum devices, representing a crucial step in the emerging field of quantum machine learning. The distorted product structure of a semi-slant submanifold was explored by Flores, et al. in 2018. Our research focuses on semi-slant submanifolds with this distorted product structure within nearly contact manifolds. We establish a main theorem, incorporating multiple formulas, which addresses the geo-mean curvature for such semi-slant submanifolds. We also identify several key conditions under which these semi-slant submanifolds are extra-closed or totally real, depending on their orientation. Our analysis encompasses the distorted product structure of reductive Hopf and lens type submanifolds. We further demonstrate the existence of such semi-slant submanifolds, utilizing a mapping cylinder construction. Lastly, a real hypersurface example illustrates that the extra-closed property does not imply minimality. Additionally, we show the existence of non-minimal, totally real hypersurfaces. Our results contribute to the understanding of pointwise semi-slant distorted product submanifolds in the context of nearly contact geometry. These discoveries not only deepen our understanding of quantum Hall systems, but also have potential implications for designing stable quantum bits. To facilitate future research, this paper provides a comprehensive overview of spectral flow and ground state regulation in both standard and modified quantum Hall systems, and offers a framework for understanding the relationship between magnetoroton spectra and ground state zero modes. Lastly, this paper conducts a thorough analysis of the numerical challenge posed by QRH systems, and suggests avenues for further research. This paper's findings are significant, not only for advancing our understanding of quantum Hall systems, but also for contributing to the development of quantum bits that are more stable and efficient. Its impact extends beyond the realm of quantum Hall systems, offering insights into the spectral flow and ground state zero modes of various gapped systems, and providing a new theoretical understanding of quantum mechanics. Initially, we convert roads into a planar graph and represent vehicles as balls moving through the graph, where their trajectories form distinct spatial clusters. By applying the geometric triangle inequality to these clusters, we derive a measurable indicator for outbreak detection and reduce outlier influence through robust statistics. Our results reveal that our algorithm outperforms existing methods in detecting clusters, detecting more outbreaks and reducing false positive rates, while also showing consistency with actual disease outbreaks in the region. Overall, our framework provides a reliable basis for analyzing disease outbreaks on sparse transportation networks. Natural language can be employed to specify objectives in reinforcement learning tasks, but its limited precision may result in multiple interpretations of the same instruction, a problem known as referential ambiguity. In natural language, the lack of grammatical context can lead to confusing similar-sounding words and indeterminate reference. Many current methods try to mitigate this issue by creating datasets with detailed instructions for ground truth values, but this approach is impractical for real-world tasks, often relying on natural language with inherent ambiguity. Instead of overcoming referential ambiguity, some methods interpret natural language objectives as a single-minded goal, neglecting alternative interpretations that might be relevant in other situations. In this paper, a new technique is proposed to overcome referential ambiguity by Leaning on Domain Knowledge - a System Designed to Reinforce Learning. The method translates domain-specific knowledge into a probabilistic model that considers multiple possible interpretations of an instruction, based on the context of related actions. This approach is demonstrated to be effective on a series of challenging tasks, including a complex game called shopping, requiring multiple dependent objectives to be simultaneously achieved. The method allows for natural language objectives to be efficiently fulfilled in environments characterized by referential ambiguity. We develop a novel method for reconstructing an arbitrary quantum channel using just shadow (trace) expectations of its output states. Our approach is versatile and can be applied across different subspaces of the input quantum system, with the channel itself being defined on any finite-dimensional subspace. Through a series of constructions, we establish that there exists a set of non-negative, unitary-invariant polynomials that fully capture the channel's behavior, even when it operates on infinite-dimensional spaces. This allows us to determine the exact number of non-negative polynomials needed for channels with a specific rank and classical reducibility. Furthermore, we define a set of inner products that can be used to extract information about a quantum channel, even when only working with states from specific subspaces. This leads to a new framework for channel tomography, with the ability to reconstruct a quantum channel using limited data and achieve the best possible reconstruction error. Our work, related to subspaces of the input quantum system, expands upon existing research by B. H. Julia-Dias et al. [Phys. Rev. Research 2, 023161, 2020]. Additionally, our method for reconstructing channels that are non-full-rank, as well as for cases with limited data, has significant practical applications in experimental channel characterization. Finally, our approach to constructing the Mumford-Schwartz coordinate has connections to recent research by F. Gao et al. [Nature Physics 16, 938, 2020]. Network centrality metrics, which gauge node importance, can be used in various applications including ranking, filtering, and predicting node behaviors.  Most existing metrics are either local (based on specific characteristics) or global (summing various characteristics) and focused on a particular scale (neighboring nodes or entire networks) with limited options for multi-scale analysis.  To address this limitation, a new metric called Gromov Centrality is developed that operates at multiple network scales by calculating a node's importance based on the shortage of the triangle inequality.  To efficiently calculate this metric for large networks, an algorithm with a computational cost proportional to $O(n\alpha(m,n))$ is designed where $\alpha(m,n)$ represents the harmonic number of the number of edges $m$ in a network with $n$ nodes.  For networks with a power-law distribution of node degrees, a variant of the algorithm is developed with a computational cost proportional to $O(n+ m\log^3 m)$.  By using the metric to analyze a model network with hierarchical structure and comparative analyses on real networks and by incorporating current metrics as special cases of Gromov Centrality, its effectiveness is demonstrated.  Results confirm its ability to characterize multi-scale network structure and accurately classify nodes according to their actual behaviors.  Furthermore, Gromov Centrality reveals new information about particular networks, notably a network related to the spread of the coronavirus in the United States.  In general, Gromov Centrality is suitable for a wide variety of network centrality applications where the focus is on a multi-scale analysis of network structure.  Moreover, its utility extends beyond just centrality metrics to the creation of additional network metrics that take into consideration the particular geometric properties of the networks in question.  To efficiently allow users to generate and calculate these new metrics, a accompanying R and Python software packages are provided.  With the capability to perform a wide variety of analytical tasks, Gromov Centrality is suitable for a wide range of network analysis applications involving the measurement of node importance at multi-scale network levels. This research explores various classifications of singular matrix pencils based on strong and weak equivalence, introducing novel categories of differential and Kronecker equivalence along with existing ones. The potential of using noisy intermediate-scale quantum computers with the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) lies in molecular simulations, where excitations are common, such as when pi orbitals are excited. The problem is that current adaptive VQE protocols, which improve sample rates and reduce overall latency, don't account for excitations and therefore aren't utilized fully. To fix this, we've developed the qubit-excitation-driven adaptive VQE (Qx-adv-VQE), which automatically switches to an alternative evolution strategy based on the presence of excitations. By simulations using model molecules, such as the acetone and pentacene, Qx-adv-VQE surpasses both the original ad-vqe and the standard es-vqe in terms of accuracy, latency, sample efficiency, and computational cost. Additionally, Qx-adv-vqe outperforms another adaptive algorithm called sequential adaptive elimination of configurations (ad-cae) in terms of accuracy and computational cost. Furthermore, the proposed method's fault-tolerance properties are studied using a reduced model and the results show that under noise as high as 2.0 percent, the cost to compute the ground state is equivalent to calling the ADV-CAE 1.5 to 2.5 times more often than necessary to achieve the same result. This shows that Qx-adv-VQE offers significant advantages over existing adaptive algorithms. To get a better understanding, we analyzed the trade-offs between accuracy, noise, cost, and computational resources and we're now exploring the extension of this concept to address other limitations in adaptive algorithms. Ultimately, the proposed method allows us to take full advantage of the potential of the VQE algorithm by maximizing learning rate variations. To support our findings, the code for the qubit-excitation-driven adaptive vqe (Qx-adv-vqe) is now publicly available at this github page. Using frozen orbitals allows us to avoid mixing to lower-lying states, which is particularly useful when debugging. However, given the difficulty of obtaining accurate MAP estimates for complex datasets like audio and vision, it has traditionally been assumed they are impractical for training generative models. These results showcase the potential benefits of accurate representation learning in various applications. Moreover, the developed model serves as a powerful diagnostic tool, providing additional insights into the model's behavior. Potential future directions in full Bayesian inference are also explored. Our analysis assesses the implications for modern cosmology of the findings reported by the NANOGrav collaborative effort, suggesting the detection of gravitational-wave background generated during inflation. We examine potential inaccuracies in calculating the binary black hole contribution to the gravitational-wave background and the GW-CDM model that assumes a constant amplitude for primordial gravitational waves across time. We find that including these inaccuracies resolves the discrepancy between NANOGrav's findings and those of the Advanced LIGO-Virgo collaboration in a manner consistent with the universe's observed tension regarding the distance ladder and Hubble constant values. Furthermore, we find that accounting for these inaccuracies results in significant consequences for cosmology, notably a lower estimate for the universe's matter density and a higher estimate for the primordial helium abundance. We find that these analytical estimates align closely with those obtained through Markov chain Monte Carlo analyses of the data from NANOGrav, Advanced LIGO-Virgo and cosmic microwave background observations. Our findings imply that an accurate determination of gravitational-wave background amplitude could reconcile the cosmic tensions mentioned above. We also find that NANOGrav's findings are sensitive to the universe's neutrino mass constraint, potentially aligning with recent mass estimates for neutrinos. The utilization of mediation analysis has expanded across numerous disciplines within social and health sciences. This method evaluates how an exposure influences an outcome through an intermediate variable, often employing logistic regression with binary outcome and mediator variables. Known problems in such contexts are over-identification, weak identification, and biased inference. This research addresses these challenges by outlining a computational approach for weakly identifying mediators in case-control settings. This method involves numerically solving a nonlinear equation system derived from maximum likelihood estimation. Additionally, we propose an alternative estimation technique based on Profile Score, along with an associated standard error calculator. Outside of logistic regression, we provide an approach for weakly identifying mediators in binomial response models. We also apply our methods to investigate the impact of education on COVID-19 infection through the Danish Crumbly Elbow method, and compare them with a machine learning-based alternative. Finally, we outline a related approach for linear structural equation models, similar to partial instrumental variable estimation techniques. Although the focus is case-control data, we show that our methods can be adapted for traditional outcome data with treatment variables. This research highlights computational innovations for analyzing mediation effects in typical social and health science applications. As such, the results are relevant to a broad range of fields, including psychology, sociology, epidemiology, and COVID-19 related fields. In an attempt to address these issues, a new theory known as Executive Ability Theory (EAT) has been developed. EAT views perceptions as a source of information and uses a comparative approach to assess value, which involves both a reconsideration of perception values and a summary of past experiences. We propose a new expectation mechanism, the Executive Ability Perceiver (EAP), which implements EAT through the integration of two processes: a resampling and relabeling process of perceptions based on feedback and a summary of past experiences. We found that EAT outperforms traditional decision theory in scenarios involving uncertainty and a changing risk environment, which are commonly found in financial decision-making situations. Furthermore, EAT exhibits more realistic assessment and decision-making patterns in various scenarios. We also provide a decision-making framework for EAT and introduce an algorithm for implementing EAP, which is available at https://github.com/jianweng2020/terminal-completion-based-EAT. The ALICE Collaboration has submitted a 10-year proposal to the European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN) to continue and expand its program. This upgrade would involve installing a completely novel detector system, incorporating new tracking and fast timing components, as well as a cutting-edge high-resolution calorimeter for impact factor studies and heavy flavor analysis. This report summarizes the key aspects of the proposed project. The upgraded ALICE detector will allow for major advancements in several areas of the program, including the exploration of hot nuclear matter through high-energy heavy-ion collisions. These goals also include the study of hadron production in proton-proton and smaller nuclear collisions, particularly in relation to the study of nucleosynthesis conventionally achieved using secondary beams. Once installed, the new detector will offer data of unprecedented quality on heavy-flavor lifetimes at LHC energies, opening up new avenues of research in quantum chromodynamics. The ALICE Collaboration's plans for theoretical research and international activities at CERN are also outlined in the proposal. The physical goals of the program are expected to be achieved through a combination of the existing and installed detector systems, as well as experiments conducted at the highest luminosity ever recorded at LHC. These experiments in minimum-bias scenarios are expected to yield approximately 100 times more data than those at fixed-target experiments operating at the same energy. As such, the ALICE Collaboration is positioned to produce highly influential results in multiple fields of research in basic nuclear physics over the next decade. This paper introduces the Multilingual Event Extraction dataset (MEE), a significant resource for researching event recognition and extraction in various languages. 
The dataset, covering six languages including English, Spanish, and four other languages, comprises 8,542 articles with embedded events from news sources online.
Each event is annotated with four key components - the happening date, describing text, affiliated organizations, and related individuals - as well as its categorization within 11 core categories.
Notably, the dataset is unique in that it not only accounts for English but also four other languages, thus presenting new hurdles for multilingual event extraction techniques.
The developers of MEE have made the dataset available online, accompanied by an implementation of its extraction method, titled Multilingual Event Extraction (MEET-2021).
Researchers can use the MEE dataset to evaluate their multilingual event extraction algorithms.
Furthermore, we have also released Multilingual Event Extraction via Cross-Linguual Transfer (MET), the first multilingual event extraction model that can handle multiple languages, and have evaluated it using the MEE dataset and dataset from TEME-2021. The results show that MET outperforms other baselines in terms of F1 measure. The multilingual event extraction model and MEE dataset are accessible at https://github.com/Allx2/MET. A fundamental task in NLP, universal parsing, aims to identify a sentence's structural and meaning components using pre-existing models. This study investigates whether strong parsing abilities can be achieved by training a single model across various languages. Initially, the research relies on the Matrix Tensor Toolkit library to implement and compare the effectiveness of affine and convolution-based models for universal parsing. Convolution models prioritize sentence structure, while affine models combine syntax and semantics more effectively. To improve model performance, additional modules are proposed, including an ELMo-based module for meaning representation and a maximum spanning tree module for enhancing structure analysis. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that a single model can achieve near-native levels of performance in parsing multiple languages. Furthermore, the research provides suggestions for future universal parsing endeavors. When using existing translation datasets, our study surpasses the current state in F1 measure for universal parsing across 8 languages, outperforms parsing results for French and German in the mTLB dataset, and rivals the results of a recently published work on universal parsing. We have made our code available on GitHub, including instructions on how to replicate our study. We hope our research and outcomes can serve as a foundation for other universal parsing investigations. We also provide enhanced parsing results for 50 languages on our project website. These results, although not as strong as some other studies, are obtained using a single model trained without language-specific data, demonstrating a compelling set of outcomes. Our research is a comprehensive study of 184 early-type galaxies with mass above
$10^{11}M_{\odot}$, identified in the HSC-DR1, focusing on tidal features derived
from the morphological analysis. Tidal features are observed in 70% of our sample,
primarily consisting of tidal tails (79%), tidal arcs (31%), and ghostly features
(21%). We calculated the flux proportion of tidal features for our sample, ranging
from 3% to 90%, observing a higher rate of features for galaxies of lower mass
($5.1\times10^{10}M_{\odot}$) at 53%, in contrast to those of higher mass ($1.1\times
10^{12}M_{\odot}$) with a feature rate of 14%. This suggests a relationship
where more massive galaxies exhibit fewer and less prominent tidal features. We
deduced a merger rate of 3.4\times10^{-13}yr^{-1} based on these findings, in
agreement with previous studies. Moreover, our data suggest a merger rate of 1.4
yr^{-1} for galaxies of mass $10^{11}M_{\odot}$. Notably, our data show that 37%
of our sample have undergone two or more recent major mergers, indicated by evident
tidal features. We observed minimal disruption from recent mergers in 53% of our
sample, consisting of features such as ring structures or enhanced star formation,
suggesting these mergers have primarily added mass rather than randomizing it. We
estimate that 14% of our sample consist of dynamically distinct double systems. We
propose the utilization of machine learning techniques to accelerate the manual
verification process for identifying tidal features in future research.

Building trust with patients, and ultimately their families, necessitates establishing open and honest relationships. This trust, referred to as 'caring trust,' is comprised of two components: the patient's confidence in being cared for (c care) and their trust in being cared about (c faith). Both elements are reciprocal in nature, influenced by and influencing the caring actions and intentions of healthcare providers. Due to its subjective and emotional character, 'caring trust' often goes unquantifiable in research studies, which tend to focus primarily on 'clinical trust,' a measure of patients' trust in healthcare professionals' competence. However, clinical trust does not directly account for patients' feelings of care and are thus considered distinct concepts. An attempt has been made to develop a quantitative metric for the 'caring trust' framework through an online survey distributed to undergraduate students, yielding results such as: Patients consider 'c care to be primarily determined by the emotional support they receive, whereas 'c faith relies more heavily on the actions and intentions of healthcare providers. An experiment incorporating a subject-level approach using incentives analyzed the effectiveness of small acts of kindness in influencing 'c faith and found that actions reflecting empathy and compassion have a more profound impact compared to other potential influencers like incentives. This study showcases an innovative methodology for discovering ethical principles through principles mining and highlights 'c faith as a suitable attribute for modeling this value in real-world scenarios. An online leaderboard was also implemented to further encourage the discovery of 'c faith-influencing features. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that Collaborative Data-Informed Modeling can facilitate the identification and modeling of complex ethical and moral variables like 'caring trust,' which can be applied in various domains, encompassing predictive modeling, optimization, and recommender systems. These findings can be applied in areas such as influencing 'c faith through social or emotional influences, optimizing campaigns aimed at improving patient care, or suggesting personalized actions to healthcare providers aimed at boosting 'c faith. More broadly, this research contributes to our understanding of quantitative measurement as a potential means of addressing moral and ethical issues. This paper presents a novel optimization technique for training quantized neural networks by extending a previously established method. The original approach, Askew, is adapted to 'approach' the optimal solution of quantized training, a concept previously explored with limited success using gradient descent. In contrast, this technique generates solutions that consistently meet the quantization constraints with minimal computational overhead. The algorithm leverages the unique properties of quantization to break down the optimization problem into manageable sub-problems and implements a novel search mechanism. The proposed approach demonstrates a significant 2.78x speedup over back-propagation and achieves an average error reduction of 42.96%, surpassing the performance of BP on the MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets. The effectiveness of Generative Adversarial Models (GANs) relies heavily on learning meaningful representations in a hidden space within a high-dimensional and non-linear mapping. Presently, most GAN architectures assume that hidden states in the mapping provide sufficient structure and clarity for the generator's output production. In our investigation, we establish that this inherent assumption is not necessarily valid and that hidden states can actually pose significant obstacles to the generator's ability to produce useful outputs. Furthermore, to address this shortcoming, we introduce a novel method known as HOC (Hidden layer Output Conditioning), which dynamically adjusts the value of the hidden states by leveraging an auxiliary context. Our experimental findings demonstrate the practical efficacy of the HOC technique in improving GAN training. Our results reveal that HOC leads to a notable improvement in the quality of the generated samples and reduces the average training loss by a significant margin of 73.12%. Additionally, samples produced by the HOC method exhibit a higher level of semantic accuracy (9% improvement) and achieve state-of-the-art results in the domain adaptation task. You can visualize the samples on an interactive website: https://hidden-conditional-gan.netlify.app/. Source code is available on GitHub: https://github.com/minsuhan/jd-GAN. We will also be presenting our findings at the Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 2021.

Step samplers are an ideal choice for sampling at distinct spatial and temporal layers because they naturally adapt to changes in the parameter space as the sampling progresses.  We investigate the potential benefits and differences in performance between using one dedicated sampler for each layer and a single generic sampler that can handle any layer when given appropriate guidance - giving rise to a four-performancerating system.  We conduct a series of practical experiments to test the step samplers under distinct conditions and find that those built upon elliptical methods, including elliptical slice sampling, perform significantly better than their counterparts.  We further improve the generic sampler, dubbed "contrast of step samplers" (COSS), by creating efficient strategies to improve its performance in various scenarios.  Through practical applications, our proposed method exhibits superior sampling efficiency when compared to other established sampling methods. In this research, a new method called DNPL is proposed to perform out-of-distribution detection by incorporating a different layer structure into the network, which consists of Normal Process Layers (NPLs). Each NPL follows the latent variable model pattern, where the generative model's prior distribution is parameterized by a Normal variational posterior distribution. During training, DNPL networks predict the distribution of inputs and measure their similarity to the distribution of inputs seen during training using the prediction loss. When predicting on out-of-distribution data, the loss will increase, indicating out-of-distribution data. DNPL achieves superior detection performance over state-of-the-art methods on diverse out-of-distribution detection tasks, including digit recognition and 2D histopathology analysis.
