Recent advancements in deep learning have led to increased interest in using alternative loss functions other than cross-entropy for task-independent supervised learning. However, the impact of these loss functions and their performance in practice remain unclear and motivated research to investigate their use. This work employs the "gradient surgery" method, which integrates theoretical optimization concepts into deep learning frameworks, to compare the performance of different loss functions in a range of shallow and deep neural networks. Our analysis examines not only the optimal solution but also the path to convergence in neural network training. Our experiments demonstrate that while some loss functions outperform cross-entropy in specific scenarios, their benefits are often negligible, and their implementation is often counterproductive. Our source code is available for public access at https://github.com/demharvey/gradient-surgery. Our study provides insights that can guide the selection of suitable loss functions for specific applications. Furthermore, the theoretical framework of our findings enables the derivation of new algorithms and methods that can be applied to train neural networks. Specifically, we derive a new algorithm, known as the Exponential Rank Maximization algorithm, which can be used for a range of loss functions and can be adapted for supervised learning. Our theoretical analysis confirms that our algorithm is capable of achieving a local convergence rate of O(1/t) under certain conditions, which is comparable to the convergence rate of gradient descent optimization in some cases. Our research framework is not limited to its current applications and provides a foundation for further exploration and development of new loss functions and optimization techniques. With an extensive array of theoretical possibilities, we identify several challenges and open questions in this area of study. Specifically, we confirm the existing result of [Kothari et al. 2020] that convex loss functions lead to suboptimal solutions that degrade as the number of neurons increases, even if the number of samples in the training dataset surpasses the number of neurons. This result highlights an important potential drawback of using task-independent loss functions, as the range of possible gradients expands in an unbounded manner. Our research provides a complete characterization of the conditions under which convex loss functions lead to suboptimal solutions and reveals that this outcome is an inherent result of the properties of convex functions and neural network training, applicable to a broad range of optimization techniques. In contrast to our initial findings, we demonstrate that non-convex loss functions do not lead to suboptimal solutions that degrade in a similar manner and show that neural network training with these loss functions can converge at a rate of O(1/t) similar to convex loss functions

In the nonrandom multi-armed bandit problem where each arm has a distinct value of a given distribution, we propose an adaptive approach. Unlike equivalent problems with random arms, this setting takes into account the positive probability of arm-specific values and the possibility of delay in choosing arms. We demonstrate that an adaptive method, SPARROW, results in a high probability bound on the expected reward loss as the number of arms grows, being only slightly worse than the optimal reward gain from knowing the exact arm values. Furthermore, SPARROW achieves similar results when the expected wait times for each arm also depend on the arm values. We extend these findings by showing that SPARROW works well even when there are a finite number of possible arm values, thus generalizing its applications. Additionally, we illustrate its usage in the context of expert problems where each arm corresponds to a prediction method with a unique loss function. We prove that SPARROW results in a high probability bound on the expected loss function loss, being only slightly worse than the minimum-expected-loss function value achievable by knowing the exact function. Furthermore, we demonstrate that an expert version of SPARROW achieves similar results when the expert services have delay times that depend on their respective performance levels. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SPARROW through comprehensive experiments on a variety of problems, supporting its theoretical validity. We also highlight its unique application in the context of stock trading, showing that SPARROW outperformed state-of-the-art methods used in the financial field. Human-written dialogue text exhibits varied characteristics in distinct stages of composition, which are influenced by factors including the intention to convey information, establish a social connection, or create a dramatic effect. To produce dialogue text akin to that written by humans, it is crucial to comprehend these characteristics and harness them effectively. Prior approaches to generating dialogue text have overlooked these variables despite their proven impact on output quality. In our research, we propose a novel end-to-end framework for learning dialogue text composition that is informed by specific social and informational goals. By applying a practical framework with adjustable parameters, we categorize the generation process into predictable stages and predict a sequence of words at each stage, all while adhering to a predictive paradigm. The framework's predictive stages allow for goal-conditioned generation and flexible multitask learning, which can be used for training and evaluating dialogue systems. In our experiments, we focus on the goal of creating a dramatic effect in dialogue, employing a goal-neutral text dataset derived from TV transcripts and using the framework to produce human-like dialogue text over various data sets in multiple languages, including English, German, and Russian. Our results demonstrate that the framework effectively addresses the challenge of producing dialogue text by leveraging naturally occurring social cues and semantic structures in dialogue, ultimately yielding high-quality output that surpasses previous competitive models. Further analysis of these results reveals that dialogue writing is a complex, multi-faceted task requiring further investigation into the factors influencing composition at different stages. The framework's code and associated data are publicly accessible at https://github.com/allenai/LEATHER. For the life-span assessment of offshore wind turbines, computational simulations generating loads due to waves, wind, and sea states in specific situations are often used to estimate fatigue life. However, conducting a vast number of simulations is necessary to achieve accurate results, which leads to extreme computational demands due to the high costs involved. Surrogate models can accelerate this process by replacing costly simulations in assessments, thereby minimizing computational times. A recent statistical approach combines multiple Gaussian Process models, each modeling the behavior of a wind turbine's response under a distinct set of input parameters, to create an accurate and non-linear model of its behavior. We have successfully applied this technique in assessments for a set of offshore wind turbines to derive accurate predictions of their survival times from simulated load cases, which took only a fraction of the original computational time required. Here, the accuracy of this statistical approach is further demonstrated through an analysis of computational efficiency and productivity in the context of offshore wind-energy engineering. Additionally, a related open-source software is introduced to facilitate its use in future applications. Furthermore, we discuss some of the remaining limitations of this statistical approach and offer a few potential solutions to expand its effectiveness and applicability. Ultimately, we aim to utilize this computational model to conduct a thorough cost-benefit analysis of advanced wind-turbine technologies with low-frequency tuned tuned masses that are designed to enhance the life-span of offshore wind turbines by as much as 10-20 years through automatic stability adjustments. A future publication will present the results of this study, which have shown that these advanced technologies can indeed contribute to significant extensions of a wind turbine's life-span. Our work highlights the vast potential for applied computational mechanics to shape the design and development of future offshore and onshore wind-energy infrastructure. Moreover, it underscores the critical role that data-driven computational mechanics can play in addressing the pressing challenges of our modern energy systems. We introduce the TRAFOS method, which determines the microscopic causes of dynamic behavior by leveraging the assumption that an object's future is equally likely to exist. This leads to a mathematical optimization problem that seeks to develop a model representing the object's history. As a result, its corresponding probability value serves as an indicator of how well the model fits the given information. As additional data becomes available, the problem is reformulated to incorporate the new data, and the method repeatedly applies this approach. We implement this method using the principle of strong stability, thereby ensuring its computationally efficient nature. We illustrate the effectiveness of this method using the example of the Lorenz tables, as well as with experiments involving realistic simulations of molecular rotation and data derived from protein dynamics studies. We demonstrate that our method provides accurate results even with limited amounts of data, and does so in a matter of seconds or minutes, depending on the specific conditions. This significantly surpasses the performance of traditional techniques used to reconstruct dynamic behavior, with the TRAFOS method exhibiting a favorable trade-off between computational cost and the need for large datasets. This represents a crucial step towards the development of data-driven models that can efficiently handle non-equilibrium processes. Furthermore, in accordance with our assumption that future states are equally likely, the method delivers an important measure of the model's accuracy, namely the Shannon entropy of the trajectory ensemble. This information can be used to gauge the method's success and monitor its progress over time. We propose that the method's ability to provide microscopic descriptions even in cases where multiple solutions exist, while also estimating the degree of uncertainty, represents a pioneering development. This represents a significant advancement, and showcases the method's potential as a universal tool for analyzing time-resolved data by leveraging the concept of trajectory ensemble. We also argue that the method's underlying theory provides a clearer understanding of the meaning and the calculation approach for Shannon entropy, as calculated using the optimization criterion in its constrained optimization problem. This represents a mathematical demonstration of the strong stability principle at work. We also show the method's local convergence properties. This represents an essential step towards the development of MRA-like schemes for analyzing time-resolved data by leveraging the concept of trajectory ensemble. We also introduce the idea of using optimization criterion as a new type of functional for this purpose. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness and its local convergence properties using the example of the Lorenz tables, as well as through simulations of molecular rotation and protein dynamics studies. Behavioral data in driving simulates real-world scenarios, guided by driving scenarios. Current databases focus on manual interactions and overlook the complexities of naturalistic driving behaviors by excluding essential factors like driving situations and fellow drivers' actions. This study presents a new dataset called SceNDD, consisting of multiple layers: a vast collection of driving situations, various driving actions, and resulting vehicle speeds across diverse scenarios. In contrast to existing datasets, SceNDD captures situations and driving behaviors in multiple locations and considers multiple factors like weather and road conditions. A large number of driving sessions have been conducted in German cities to collect the data, consisting of over 35 driving situations and nearly 5,000 laps. To facilitate practical applications, this study introduces two advanced models: Situation-based Modular Policy and Situation-aware Non-Decision Making. Both models utilize the SceNDD structure to demonstrate improved performance compared to traditional Non-Decision Making approaches, showcasing promising results in offline and online evaluations. Moreover, MMs based on SceNDD outperform current state-of-the-art methods, highlighting the importance of driving situations in naturalistic driving behaviors. Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces (RISs) have gained significant attention due to their potential to dynamically control the communication signal's path, making RIS-supported systems appealing for diverse environments and applications. Nonetheless, the RIS-related channel estimation challenge remains unresolved. Current models used for RIS channel estimation include a standard, insufficiently extended inverse discrete Fourier transform (IDFT) model, a standard, excessively extended modulated complementary cumulative distribution function (MCCDF) model, a standard low complexity model, and a standard, incomplete RIS low complexity model. These models, however, fail to consider the real-world RIS hardware impairments (HWIs) that are critical in RIS systems. In our research, an enhanced least squares (ELLS) algorithm is proposed to estimate and recover the RIS channel with limited CP and HWIs. The proposed ELLS algorithm outperforms the existing methods by leveraging additional latent features to reconstruct the RIS channel, resulting in superior performance in terms of channel correlation and average squared error (ASE) values. The theoretical latency of the ELLS algorithm is analyzed and compared with the existing models, showing significant improvement with reduced latency. Moreover, the average energy required to achieve a specified ASE value is also analyzed and compared, demonstrating substantial energy savings while maintaining superior performance in the presence of HWIs. The effectiveness of the ELLS algorithm is validated through simulated RIS-OFDM system tests. Notably, the ELLS algorithm successfully estimates the RIS channel with minimal CP and HWIs, showcasing its potential as a low complexity solution for RIS-OFDM systems and beyond. The simulated results reveal that the ELLS algorithm outperforms the existing models in terms of ASE values and latency even when the CP is extended to 20\%. Furthermore, the ELLS algorithm successfully generalizes to non-Gaussian RIS channels and non-ideal HWIs, highlighting its practical applications and usability in real-world communication systems. The ELLS algorithm source code is publicly available for research purposes at the specified repository, allowing the research community to reproduce the results, modify the code, and utilize it for further advancements in the field of RIS-aided communication systems. The theoretical models and average energy analysis show that the ELLS algorithm significantly outperforms the existing models in terms of both ASE values and latency, effectively reducing the computational complexity and energy consumption while maintaining superior performance in the presence of HWIs. We have developed a new approach to the established integral fluctuation theorem for single energy experiments, which analyzes the connection between the stored and released energy of a system over an extended period. By analyzing the exponential decay of the theorem's left-hand side, we demonstrate its application to non-invasive measurements of the system's energy. We also introduce a new theoretical framework to predict the lower bound of the exponential decay rate. This theoretical framework relies on the linear response principle and the assumption that the system's relaxation is primarily driven by its stored energy. Furthermore, we verify the accuracy of our theoretical framework through simulations of an active rotor and an active particle in a harmonic trap. Finally, we conduct experiments validating the application of the theoretical framework to non-invasive measurements of the system's energy. Our findings support the application of the theoretical framework to single energy experiments and confirm that the exponential decay rate is sensitive to the system's energy characteristics. Overall, the developed theoretical framework provides valuable insights into the system's energy dynamics and can be employed to evaluate the effectiveness of energy harvesting technologies. The experiments and simulations in this study contribute to the development of a general theoretical framework for single energy experiments and their application to both non-invasive and invasive assessments of the system's energy. The developed theoretical framework offers theoretical support for the application of fluctuation theorems in the assessment of energy and can be employed to evaluate the effectiveness of energy harvesting devices through experimental and simulation studies. Based on the experimental and simulation results, we have established a solid connection between the exponential decay rate and the average stored energy of the system over an extended period. We have also verified that under relaxed conditions, the exponential decay rate is determined by the average of the stored and released energy of the system. Using the established criteria, we have demonstrated that the rotor's efficiency can be improved by adjusting its characteristics, specifically by increasing its moment of inertia and compressibility. We are exploring the deformation space of G2-instants on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between G2-instantons and certain tangent vector fields on the group G2 that leave the structure with skew-symmetric (3,4)-tensor invariant. For the specific case of a 7-dimensional sphere with S1-symmetry, the deformation space of G2-instantons can be directly associated with S1-cohomology in degree 2, resulting in an infinite-dimensional deformation space. Additionally, when the 7-dimensional sphere is transformed into a 3-Sasakian manifold with S1-symmetry, the deformation space of G2-instantons dimensionally reduces to the hypercenter of its structure, leading to a finitely dimensional deformation space. Using an obstruction tensor, we have developed a criterion for the existence of the deformation of G2-instantons and have demonstrated its relevance in the specific case of a 7-dimensional nilmanifold where the deformation space of G2-instantons can be directly associated with the first cohomology group. Our research provides new possibilities for constructing the deformation of G2-instantons, especially among the S1-symmetry manifolds. A direct application of our findings has been demonstrated through the example of a 5-sphere. The global spread of the coronavirus has led many countries to adopt a surveillance approach by using mobile data to track and contain the virus spread, which has raised significant privacy concerns despite the benefits of control measures. To address these concerns, researchers have proposed the use of contact tracing techniques such as proximity detection using sensors (gyro, accelerometer, accelerometer) and location tracking, which can be enhanced by contact tracing technology (CTT). Although prior studies have analyzed the privacy issues associated with mobile COVID-19 contact tracing apps, the feasibility and privacy implications of using device sensors to track individuals have been left unexplored, which is particularly concerning as sensor data can reveal users' personal activities. This research aims to bridge this gap by developing a framework that uses machine learning to identify sensitive moments, demonstrating the effectiveness of this method in preserving user anonymity in the process of contact tracing. A suspicious activity detection model was developed using deep learning techniques, which were tested on data from over 600 users comprising typical urban users, dancers, and professional contact tracers. The results showed that the model could accurately identify sensitive moments with high precision, which are currently identifiable with low precision. By leveraging these improvements, the study proposes a method to preserve user confidentiality in CTT-based coronavirus surveillance systems. Importantly, the study highlights the need to re-evaluate the current CTT-based coronavirus surveillance systems and the potential for this technology to be adapted for other public health purposes while mitigating the collection of sensitive personal data. The framework's source code is publicly available at https://github.com/gustavolc/computationalprivacy. Recently, significant interest has been generated among researchers and physicists by quantum-inspired deep learning methods. These techniques employ mathematical structures derived from quantum physics to develop highly effective deep neural networks. This paper delves into various approaches used to implement quantum effects in neural networks and explores their underlying justifications. Additionally, we will review current research outcomes and discuss potential roads for further exploration in this emerging field. Finally, we will outline the main challenges posed by quantum algorithms and describe the ongoing efforts to address them. Alongside theoretical advancements, we will highlight the experimental progress being made in applying quantum-inspired deep learning methods to solve real-world problems. The paper will conclude with an examination of the current division between quantum machine learning and quantum computing, and we will propose a future research pathway that combines these fields with classical deep learning to create innovative machine learning methods. This research paper introduces a tool for automatically translating ACL2 representations of C code into executable C code and verifying its correctness through the creation of accompanying ACL2 theorems. The tool operates by translating the ACL2 representation into intermediate, abstract syntax tree representations in ACL2, which are then translated into C code. The tool relies on a shallow embedding of C within ACL2, leveraging the (CFLAMES Utilities) library to facilitate the analysis and verification of C code within ACL2. The tool was demonstrated in the context of developing scalable data structure implementations, such as a basic hash table and a heap data structure, which were found to be free from common errors thanks to the automatic verification provided by the tool. The tool's source code and a comprehensive tutorial on its use are both freely accessible online. The tutorial provides step-by-step guidance in utilizing the tool to develop and verify both ACL2 functions and C code. The tool was designed to address a persistent challenge in system and network programming, namely, the lack of weak consistency in distributed system components, with the aim of promoting the development of correct and free-from-bugs C code. The tool's potential extends to the development of both proof-driven and specification-based software, potentially expanding to other programming languages in the future. The tool's key distinction from existing research lies in its ability to generate both C code and its accompanying ACL2 theorems in a single, automated manner. The tool was successfully tested on various hash table and heap data structure implementations, which were found to be correct and free from bugs upon manual verification. The tool was utilized in a manner that resulted in both its code and generated theorems being deemed 'perfectly clear' according to the standards of the ACL2 community, which holds the tool's code and generated theorems in high esteem. The tool was found to outperform existing software verification tools, in particular a tool called ACL2gC, which was found to struggle with the tool's more complex specifications, ultimately failing to generate theorems for the tool's more complex hash table and heap data structure implementations. A detailed comparison between the tool and ACL2gC was conducted, which revealed the tool's source code to be significantly larger in size than ACL2gC, despite both tools sharing a common goal of automatically translating ACL2 representations of C code into executable C code and verifying its correctness. The tool was found to be the first evidence of shallow embeddings of C within ACL2, which was found to be sufficiently robust and stable to facilitate the analysis and verification

This study undertakes a detailed examination of two outer asteroids, recently discovered to be in a near-resonance interaction with the planet Mars. The focus is on 39991 Iochroma and its co-orbital companions Aneas and Mab. Calculations are based on a complex, phase-space map that incorporates terms to analyze various degree and order resonances up to a high truncation order. The outcomes of these calculations reveal how these resonances disrupt Iochroma's motion around Mars. The findings will be used to explain observed irregularities in Iochroma's motion and seek a plausible connection to its formation story. The study also considers the possibility of similar disruptions in the motion of another asteroid, that of Coorbital asteroid (524) Fidelia. The combination of these two outcomes may offer an explanation for the recent discovery of a near-resonance interaction between Fidelia and Mars, specifically the (3438) 1995) coorbital family. The findings will reveal key insights into the dynamics involved and offer new understanding of the respective asteroid families' formation processes. The study particularly highlights and interprets a specific hysteresis phenomenon associated with the (3,5) resonance within the Iochroma family, a feature initially reported by V. V. Kozyrev, though was not properly explained at the time. The following reasons for the appearance of this hysteresis are offered as a part of the resonance's analytical solution in the presented study. The reasons are as follows: the appearance of hysteresis is due to the resonance's switching in the Iochroma family as a result of its complex interior hysteresis phenomenon resulting from the interaction with the (3,5)-5 scenario; or the hysteresis is triggered by the resonance shift in the Iocha, not Iochroma, due to their near-equal sizes. Moreover, a similar hysteresis phenomenon has also detected in the Coorbital asteroid (524) Fidelia, indicating the hysteresis phenomenon has already occurred in the asteroid as a result of the (3,5)-5 scenario. The study also demonstrates the significance of considering the role of the Solar spin-down effect in developing theoretical models of asteroid motion. Leveraging this expression and a novel application of Ramanujan's continued product for the gamma function, we establish a generalisation of Ramanujan's continued product for the odd zeta values. Furthermore, our integral representation serves as a functional equation alternative to the given zeta function. Additionally, our findings provide continued products for specific combinations of odd and even zeta values. Lastly, similar approaches can be employed to generate continued products for a broader range of zeta functions. However, it is unclear whether these methods are applicable to the Bailey-Daquesies-Heegner zeta function. Conversely, in an appendix, we demonstrate that the Appell Hypergeometric 2_f(s) is equivalently expressible as a Hurwitz zeta function. Furthermore, we establish that it serves as a model for circle equivariant cohomology of the given representation. This paper outlines a proposed research program, detailing how techniques from algebraic topology can be utilized in physics through machine learning methods. We establish connections between traditional notions in algebraic topology and the principles of deep learning, including the connection between homotopy groups and convolutional neural networks. We provide justification for the potential success of combining these areas, referring to existing research for further support. Finally, some potential research questions and challenges are presented that could drive the development of new machine learning applications in physics.

Within the framework of nonrelativistic QCD, we have thoroughly examined the order-$\alpha_s^2$ corrections to the angular distributions of the $J/\psi$ meson in the $e^+ e^- 	o J/\psi + \eta_c, \chi_{cJ}$ processes. By employing nonrelativistic Coulomb potentials to calculate the four-body and five-body integrals involving $\alpha_s$ and momentum space anharmonics up to the order of $\alpha_s^4$, we have obtained a complete set of limit expressions that are necessary for further use in leading order perturbation theory. Subsequently, using these order-$\alpha_s^2$ corrections and the leading order expressions, we have evaluated the experimental and theoretical predictions for the $J/\psi$ angular distributions at $\sqrt{s} \approx 10.6$ GeV in the $\chi_{c1}$ energy range. Specifically, our predictions for $\alpha_s = 0.24$ align with the experimental charmonium angular distributions observed in the $\chi_{c1}$ energy range reported by the BESIII Collaboration. Furthermore, the integration of our angular distribution model and a $\sqrt{s}$-dependent value of $\alpha_s$ will enable the precise quantification of the mass splitting between the $J/\psi$ and $\chi_{c1}$ in the future. Additionally, the calculated order-$\alpha_s^2$ corrections for the $J/\psi$ angular distributions in the $\eta_c$ energy range are expected to be utilized in the determination of its mass value by the BESIII and Belle Collaborations. Ultimately, the calculated angular distributions can be used to test the experimental mass values of the $\eta_c$ and $J/\psi$ mesons as well as the mass splitting between the $J/\psi$ and $\chi_{c1}$ in the $\chi_{c1}$ energy range.

Our research delves into how everyday Signal users understand the concept of PINs.
We analyzed comments from 200,000 people who participated in a non-anonymous survey regarding their experiences with the app, discovering that users are unsure of the purpose of PINs.
Only a small percentage of users (8%) reported using a PIN, and those who did were largely aware of its function.
Conversely, users who didn't utilize a PIN expressed confusion and distrust, frequently deactivating their accounts.
From these findings, we establish that securing communications depends on trust's presence, rather than intensity.
Consequently, we suggest implementing a more straightforward PIN setup process that might improve user comprehension and boost adoption rates for our target audience. Our study offers insights for other privacy-focused messaging apps to understand their users' experiences and improve their security features accordingly. Ultimately, we aim to contribute to enhancing the security of communications for your average Signal user. 

Please note that the unencrypted survey responded to by users includes questions about their use of the second factor, i.e., PINs.
Our analysis only considers participants who provided answers to all relevant questions.
It's also worth noting that users' actual PIN statuses might differ from their self-reported responses due to the possibility of underreporting.
To mitigate potential biases, we used tripling in our analysis: asking about the second factor directly, inquiring whether users set up any second factors, and examining the second factor usage among those who claimed to have enabled PINs.
Hence, our findings are conservative and might overestimate the actual percentage if there's a discrepancy between self-reported responses and actual behaviors. 

Our research highlights Signal PINs' notable distinctions from other security features.
Firstly, it's uncommon for PINs to be used even among users who have enabled them.
Secondly, the primary reason for not using a PIN isn't that users find it too complicated to set one up - actually the majority reported it wasn't difficult at all to do so.
Thirdly, the primary reasons for not using a PIN weren't related to the ease of setting one up but rather a lack of understanding among users regarding the purpose of PINs.
If potential users feel uncertain about using a security feature, they are less likely to utilize it.
This study offers a fresh perspective on understanding why users adopt or reject security features.
It also offers a useful data point for product designers to consider when creating second-factor setup processes for their apps.

This work addresses the need for precise numerical integration in the calculation of solar-phase integrals that appear extensively in the analysis of theoretical solar spectra. The integrands typically involve mathematical functions and their products with a radiative source function modeled after a Lorentzian profile, to account for the limited sensitivity of available data. The required integration is over product sets of domain intervals, one for wavelength $\lambda$ ranging from 150nm to 300nm, and one for solar zenith angles $\theta$ ranging from 0 to $\pi$. The approximation of integrals is initially considered acceptable if relative errors are below 10$^{-4}$. To achieve this level of accuracy, the quadrature approach with 25-fold Gaussian integration in both the $\lambda$ and $\theta$ domains is shown to be effective. In addition to its simplicity, this method offers the advantage of being able to compute directly from raw spectral data without intermediate processing. The proposed approach also enables the computation of integrals for arbitrary zenith angles and wavelengths outside the specified ranges. The integration method can just as easily be applied to other types of radiative source functions, such as those modeled after Voigt and pseudo-Voigt profiles. The provided Fortran code includes functions for computing the needed weights and points, as well as the execution of solar-phase integrals. The code is also available in a Fortran version, known as SGQC, and can be downloaded from the repository at https://github.com/apatiw95/solar_gaussian_quadrature. The Fortran version of this code is also compatible with the C++ language. However, obtaining and utilizing curvature information is often a computationally costly process. A viable, though often underutilized strategy is to utilize approximate second-order approximations derived from the Hessian matrix or generalized Gauss-Newton approximations for optimization problems with nonlinear least squares objectives. While these approximations can be computed at a reduced cost due to shared linear components, they may not always accurately reflect the underlying complex structure of modern problems. We propose a novel structure, referred to as ViViT, that captures the inherent diminished structure of the generalized Gauss-Newton Hessian and makes it amenable for efficient computation through a newly developed Hessian-free approach. This approach encompasses a theoretical framework that encompasses prior methods, including CNN-based methods, and identifies the minimal computational requirements for implementing these methods. Using this framework, we successfully demonstrate the effectiveness of our new structure on various deep learning tasks in vision and language. Our results highlight the importance of exploiting the diminished structure for achieving this goal and showcase the superiority of our new structure over existing methods across multiple metrics. Furthermore, we showcase the applicability of our newly developed approach to a diverse range of optimization problems that do not fit into the generalized Gauss-Newton criteria, thus potentially making it a viable option for a much broader range of optimization problems and use cases. The code for our approach is made available at the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/Alkama ViViT. The experimental results from various applications demonstrate that leveraging the diminished structure of the generalized Gauss-Newton Hessian can lead to better performance and computational efficiency, thereby making it a valuable tool for optimizing various complex problems. This research demonstrates the potential benefits of exploiting the diminished structure for a range of optimization problems and showcases a novel structure for generalized Gauss-Newton approximations with improved computational efficiency. While our approach focuses on optimization algorithms for nonlinear least squares problems, we identify a broader set of applicable problems and propose that our technique could be adapted for a more general class of optimization problems with similar structure and requirements. Using a Hessian-free approach, we successfully apply our newly developed structure to various deep learning tasks in vision and language, thereby making it a valuable tool for optimizing these complex problems. Ultimately, our research emerges as a promising solution for efficient second-order optimization in the future. In languages that specify grammatical gender, related nouns with the same label differ based on the gender they represent. This paper investigates how the gender of nouns is reflected in their word embeddings, evaluating various embedding models for accuracy in distinguishing gender and finding that a particular technique is effective in most cases. It demonstrates that class-based representations capture the link between words and their underlying grammatical context, taking into account the influence of morphology, whereas singular and plural forms of words reveal consistency in their meaning patterns. Furthermore, the paper considers the implications of developing this category of embeddings and explores the potential for part-of-speech filtering to improve accuracy in most cases, while acknowledging that there are some parts of speech where distinguishing gender is particularly challenging. Ultimately, the paper presents a variety of potential applications for these gender-aware embeddings and suggests that future research should examine its broader potential across multiple languages. This study utilizes various datasets across multiple languages, including Spanish, Italian, and Greek, in its assessment of word embeddings and their accuracy in distinguishing gender. The associated code and data for this study can be accessed on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/jayakushal/ne-grammatical-gender. The study employs the following metrics to evaluate the accuracy of embeddings: mean average precision and mean average recall. The study finds a higher threshold of performance using embeddings that combine morphology and syntax, specifically 0.2881 (supporting information in Spanish). The study makes the following contributions to research in this field: It proposes accurate embeddings of gender for most parts of speech in multiple languages, improving upon prior research with more comprehensive and multi-lingual findings, as well as developing and testing embeddings of syntax and morphology that are also contextually rich. The study also presents and releases these gender-aware embeddings, providing solutions to practical issues in multiple languages that are informed by the link between words and their underlying grammatical context. The study considers the potential limitations of its findings and suggests areas of improvement, while acknowledging its broader implications and potential applications in multiple languages. The study is written in English and employs plain language summaries, while its code and data can be accessed on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/jayakushal/ne-grammatical-gender. The related numerical findings are provided in the study's appendix. The study is approved by the University of Oxford's ethics committee with reference number ETH1604- البرمجة-001. In fact, we use charmability to prove the strong Etale fundamental group rigidity of reductive groups, building on a previous finding by Gabber and Kapranov. Estimating the pose of individual objects within images is a critical task in areas like robotics and visual surveillance, with applications extending to categorizing and removing hazardous materials like hazardous chemicals and explosives. However, the task is complex due to challenges in training data, inaccuracies in object detection, and limited availability of annotation for pose estimation. In response to these issues, we present a technique to predict object poses at levels ranging from coarse to precise, all without requiring additional annotation. This technique relies on object categorization instead of relying on 2D or 3D landmarks for accuracy. Still, coarse-pose estimates benefit from knowing the general orientation of objects. As a result, we also introduce an approach to co-pose estimation, allowing us to predict both object category and pose at zero-shot levels. Our technique outperforms current state-of-the-art models by significant margins on the PASCAL3D+ dataset. Additionally, we provide detailed analysis in our study on the challenges of evaluating zero-shot class-level pose estimation. Our code and techniques are available for public access.

Predicting future traffic patterns is essential to minimize transportation delays and improve route optimization. However, forecasting traffic flow two days in advance is a highly challenging task within the transportation science community. To address this obstacle, this paper proposes an innovative spatiotemporal framework that aims to forecast the relative speed of vehicles along a highway for the next two days. To achieve this goal, the proposed method utilizes similarity analysis between the target prediction areas and other locations through support vector regression. This allows the model to identify similarities between the speed of vehicles and include predicting features, such as weather and traffic events. To maintain sparsity in the feature space, the paper adopts Optimum-Path Forest (OPF) as the regression kernel's loss function. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed method, the authors tested it using real-world data collected from Colorado State University's OTRI system. As a result, the proposed method successfully forecasts the relative speed of vehicles two days in advance with minimal error. Furthermore, the proposed method outperformed existing baseline models such as Deep State Space Models and ARIMA. The source code for the proposed framework is publicly available at https://github.com/fengleru/Similar-SFP.EXT.2022. Additional information can be found at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V7Qk8u8pY8g. The experimental outcomes demonstrate that utilizing similarity-based regression to forecast the future relative speed of vehicles results in minimal error. This research illustrates the importance of identifying predicting features that are highly correlated with the target prediction area. By leveraging these features, the proposed framework achieves significant error reduction when forecasting the future relative speed of vehicles. Ultimately, the proposed method demonstrates the potential to develop highly effective sparse traffic flow models that can alleviate transportation delays. One of the significant benefits of using sparse regression in this context is that it offers an alternative approach for training deep learning models that require large datasets. By utilizing the proposed method, the authors were able to achieve sparsity in a linear regression model without assuming Gaussian data. Furthermore, the proposed method's predictive error can be explained using two key factors: 1) the similarity between the speed of vehicles in the training dataset and the target prediction area, and 2) the sparsity of the features used to predict the future relative speed of vehicles. As shown in the results, the proposed method successfully predicts the relative speed of vehicles two days in advance with minimal error, demonstrating its potential to develop highly effective traffic flow models that can alleviate transportation delays. The REALtime Transient Collector, the back-end system of the LoFAR antenna array, can perform a comprehensive spectral analysis on the processed data with an updated interval of approximately 30.53 s, allowing for the detection of intense pulses within a relatively narrow band of 80 MHz with a frequency resolution of about 8.33 kHz. By examining the LoFAR Irish station's REALTA system over a period of 106 days, the system successfully identified a total of 12,921 high-intensity pulses, of which 7 were previously discovered SGR 1930+38 gigahertz-pulse sources and 4 were pulsar signals. Additionally, the REALTA system detected 1,972 high-intensity pulses that could not be linked to a specific astronomical source, referred to as Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs), and further analysis of these mysterious signals is needed. It's worth noting that during the observed period, REALTA detected approximately 80 percent of potential FRBs in a given hour, with an upper limit on their intensity set at $5.4\times10^{20}$ erg per second within a frequency range of 170-230 MHz. With regards to FRB detection capabilities, REALTA identified five new sources, bringing the total number of known FRBs detected at the Irish LoFAR station to eleven, with the potential to discover more during the ongoing and future data analysis processes. Moreover, the upper limit on the frequency chirp rate for detected FRBs was found to be approximately $10^{4}$ Hz per second, with an associated half-width half magnitude dispersion measure value of about $2\times10^{3}$ per second squared Hertz per second, with an upper limit set at approximately $10^{9}$ per second squared Hertz. Auxiliary frequency regulation through stabilization of voltage dynamics plays a crucial role in modern power networks. Recent shifts in energy landscapes and the rise of distributed energy sources have led to an increased need for frequency regulation. We examine a particular instance of this problem involving a small electrical network consisting of several nodes and an inverter based on supercapacitors. We derive a parametric range for the inverter's power characteristics such that the network's voltage dynamics converge towards a set equilibrium point governed by a specific nonlinear equation, allowing for easy tracking of auxiliary frequency regulation services through stabilization of the voltage dynamics. We also showcase the effectiveness of this approach in the actual demonstration of auxiliary frequency regulation services by testing it on a tiny-scale network modeled after a real-world scenario. We validate the proposed method's reliability and usability in particular and potentially it can be applied on larger scale networks consisting of various types of inverters consisting of Supercapacitor, Battery and Fuel Cell. We believe that this technique could possibly be extended for scaling up to even more complex systems and networks. We also highlight some potential obstacles that need to be addressed for implementation purposes. We convey our findings through an edited video recording of the actual demonstration. This work centers around a wireless recharge network (WRN) that incorporates intelligent surfaces (IRS) to enhance the reception quality of receivers in the presence of interfering signals and weak line-of-sight (LoS) links. However, when a strong LoS link exists between the transmitter and one receiver, it hampers the ability of IRS to optimize its element values, thus reducing overall network efficiency. In our research, we examine two scenarios: IRStoreceiver and receiverToIRS. In IRStoreceiver, we find the optimal IRS configuration that maximizes overall network throughput, but it's compromised when a LoS link is introduced between the transmitter and the target receiver. To counter this issue, we train a neural network to bypass the need for time-consuming iterative algorithms. Specifically, we use unsupervised learning to create a neural network that optimally places its activation function weights to enhance throughput, with the added benefit of also improving IRS throughput at receivers without receiver action. On the other hand, receiverToIRS involves IRS-receiver pairs, with the added constraint that IRS-receiver pairs cannot exceed half the number of total IRS elements. In this scenario, we propose a new neural network that simultaneously determines its activation function weights and number of elements for each embedded IRS, with the added constraint that certain receivers cannot enhance their throughput beyond a certain threshold. Our research indicates that these neural networks significantly outperform conventional methods, with the added benefit of also improving other throughput metrics in the network. Moreover, these neural networks can be quickly trained on small training datasets, with the added ability to seamlessly transfer to new untested scenarios. Our research, specifically verified using simulated wireless charged network elements, confirms that these neural networks significantly enhance the overall throughput of the network. Moreover, when put into practical testing, these neural networks are found to efficiently work in real-world environments with a wide variety of wireless charged network elements. In summary, these neural networks offer a practical solution to enhancing the overall efficiency of wireless charged networks, with the added ability to further improve other key throughput metrics in the network. Our research appears to be the first to propose the use of unsupervised learning to improve the overall efficiency of wireless charged networks, with particular emphasis on the added efficiency gains achieved using this method to enhance IRS element values when embedded within devices. Our research through the use of simulated and put-to-the-test real-world scenarios confirms that this method significantly improves the overall efficiency of wireless charged networks, with the added ability to further improve other key throughput metrics in the network. All Toda conformal field models have a fundamental mathematical structure derived from integrable representations of $\hat{\mathfrak{sl}_n}$ Lie algebras. In this research, we focus on the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda model, focusing on two distinct types of conformal field theories denoted as type II, which is defined by $\mathfrak{g}=\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}_3}$ and $\mathfrak{h}=\mathfrak{sl}_3$. Our aim is to identify a suitable extension of Kac-Rashov's results on weak intertertification Ward identities within the context of the type II $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda model, which has previously been extensively studied by other authors. Additionally, we prove new Ward identities associated with strong intertertification and demonstrate how these identities are closely linked to the monodromy and quantum spin change under specific twists of the type II model. This connection highlights the type II model's distinctive characteristics that set it apart from the more conventional $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ current Ward identities derived from Gaudin magnets. We utilize the type II model's fermionic representation developed by Kang-Yang to establish the new Ward identities and derive the energy-momentum tensor and conformal field operators' intertwiner conditions as a direct result. These intertwiner conditions have significant implications in the context of the type II model and serve as a fundamental aspect of this conformal field theory. We ultimately verify that the type II model's intertertification Ward identities do not apply, which is consistent with Kac-Rashov's findings for the type I $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ Toda model. Prior to this research, the type II model and its distinct Ward identity characteristics remained unknown in the scientific literature. We have successfully addressed this knowledge gap and established a novel connection between the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory and the principles of integrable representation. This connection has far-reaching consequences that can be observed in the context of the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory's fermionic representation as well as its relation to the more conventional type I $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ Toda model. As image generation technology progresses, it has become essential to evaluate the accuracy of generated images in terms of their semantic relationships with real images. To address this requirement, we introduce a novel Relation GAN (RGAN) that utilizes the relational understanding from Relation Networks to facilitate a more nuanced comparison between synthetic and natural images. RGAN outperforms prior GAN approaches in producing high-quality images and establishes a stronger connection by capturing intricate semantic relationships between the worlds of real and synthetic images. Notably, RGAN's effectiveness is enhanced when trained with a triplet loss, which improves the stability of the training process and enables precise representation of image similarities and differences. To facilitate easier hyperparameter selection, we present ColorGAN, a user-friendly tool that allows RGAN to automatically adjust its hyperparameters based on color palettes and achieve superior results. By leveraging human-annotated color theories, ColorGAN aids in the effective training of RGAN and obtaining superior generated images and semantic relationships. Ultimately, we validate the significance of semantic relationships in image understanding through a series of experiments and theoretical analyses, while demonstrating the practical applications of RGAN and ColorGAN in multiple real-world scenarios including image-to-image translation, image editing, and semantic image generation. Currently widely-used quantum key distribution (QKD) systems rely on the unique properties of single photons in bulk optics, requiring complex real-time phase stabilization to generate keys. Conversely, dual-field QKD offers a promising solution by harnessing the benefits of quantum optics within the photonic crystal QKD framework, thus eliminating the need for phase control. Building upon this concept, we present an experimental demonstration and thorough analysis of the dual-field QKD scheme without phase stabilization, showcasing its practical capabilities in real-world applications and mitigating potential issues arising from the absence of phase control. Our results obtained through experimental measurements prove that dual-field QKD systems remain secure despite the absence of phase stabilization, thus offering considerable advantages over traditional bulk-based QKD systems. Furthermore, the theoretical capabilities of dual-field QKD to reach long-distance transmission thresholds have also been explored. Our experimental findings validate the theoretical predictions, confirming the feasibility of dual-field QKD in long-distance applications without the need for phase control. In summary, the dual-field QKD scheme without phase stabilization presents a vital and innovative approach to generating secure keys in practical applications, eliminating the need for expensive and complex real-time phase control. This promising development offers considerable potential for streamlining dual-field QKD systems and achieving greater practicality in long-distance applications. Our work draws parallels between dual-field QKD and other photonic crystal-based QKD schemes that may also offer similar advantages. Understanding and evaluating the trade-offs between distance and interference-induced key generation error is crucial for determining the performance limits of dual-field QKD schemes without phase control. Our experimental findings have directly addressed this critical parameter in dual-field QKD systems. Our study further highlights the unique properties of dual-field QKD systems in long-distance applications and identifies a vital factor, the coherence time of the source, as the primary distance determinant. Our analysis reveals that the coherence time of the source directly impacts the performance of dual-field QKD systems without phase control. We have obtained experimental results validating this critical understanding of dual-field QKD systems. Our work has also explored the practical applications of coherence unit as a source coherence time metric in dual-field QKD systems. Our study indicates that dual-field QKD systems without phase control can achieve similar levels of performance as bulk-based QKD systems with real-time phase control. Time series analysis is a critical component of numerous field across data sciences, including economics, astronomy and geography. Although numerous existing tools in R provide comprehensive functionality for time series analysis, a key limitation arises from the need to integrate and sync multiple packages. To address this issue, we introduce the theft package - a collection of 27 previously "stolen" functions from various popular time series packages - thereby streamlining time series processing. As an example of the effectiveness of this approach, we showcase the implementation of multiple concurrent scale analysis and detrended fluctuation analysis using the theft package. Furthermore, we provide step-by-step instructions on using the package to run these two key time series analyses. The theft package is fully compatible with popular time series and data visualization tools in R, including ts, zoo, zygy, ggplot2 and broom. The package is also freely downloadable from CRAN. The intention is to create an all-encompassing platform for time series processing - what I am calling the MotherShip of Time Series in R. Furthermore, we determine that the expansion of $N(\lambda)$ has a unique, leading constant, subleading term to be $-\frac{I}{\sqrt{\lambda}}$, and reveal the origin of this term from the contributions of spherically symmetric harmonic fields, confirming a conjecture by Brauer. The proof involves applying the method of parametrization, linked to Friedlander and Hastie's work on perturbations of the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map. Moreover, we obtain an estimate for the expansion of the asymptotic period function of Steklov eigenvalues, following an approach from Friedlander and Hintz's analysis of the Laplace spectrum. This research is an adaptation from the findings of the case in higher dimensions, presented in our previous study. Lastly, through an additional investigation, we find the asymptotic form of the sum of the Steklov eigenvalues, verifying Riemann's famous result that the sum of eigenvalues is one-fourth the area of a nearly spherical manifold multiplied by $\lambda^{\frac{2}{3}}\log\lambda$. The investigation also yields a simplified, precise formula for calculating the sum of Steklov eigenvalues for general manifolds from any dimension $d$, above $2\lambda^{\frac{2}{d}}$. Notably, the formula is applicable to the three-dimensional case and, when inserted into a previously established inequality, results in the tightest known upper bound for the counting function $N(\lambda)$. This term would equal the integral of the gradient dot product of the vector field $X$ from its Schrödinger operator with itself, where $X$ represents harmonic fields, divided by the frequency $\lambda$. The Collatz Conjecture is a mathematical hypothesis that has withstood testing for over 80 years, having been proven true for nearly all numbers within its realm, with the exception of a set of unproven statements referring to sequences of 2^x mod 5^2 = 4. This hypothesis suggests that if a number is subjected to a series of operations - namely, doubling its value and then taking the integer part of this doubled amount, or multiplying it by 1/3 - it will ultimately reach 1, with the sequence of operations it follows being known as the Collatz Orbit. This paper seeks to shed light on why the conjecture has been proven successful for nearly all numbers, as well as provide calculations and visualizations to help illustrate its principles in a graphical context, with the goal of inspiring further research into the Collatz Conjecture and its broader mathematical implications. Determining the category of a complex STEM document is a challenging task in the field of text classification, particularly when applying linguistic features alone is insufficient for differentiation. For instance, categorizing a STEM document as physics or mathematics depends more on the underlying scientific concepts rather than surface-level language. In our study, a weighted graph representation of documents is explored, where nodes represent entities extracted from the text and edges signify mutual associations between them. This novel approach enables us to model document categorization from a distinct, semantics-driven perspective. Semantics-based document categorization allows us to identify the dominant concepts unique to each category and offers a thorough explanation of the categorization process. To adopt this approach, we developed MathBench, a comprehensive dataset categorizing STEM texts as mathematics or physics. We employed a combination of natural language processing and symbolic mathematics representation techniques to create comprehensive entity graphs from which we extracted a weighted ranking of math entities. This ranking served as the primary input for our Graph Neural Network (GNN) model, designed to handle graph data efficiently. Our experiments demonstrate that our GNN model, in combination with the math entity graph, achieves impressive accuracy on MathBench, outperforming existing linguistic features-based classifiers. Moreover, we show that our approach results in transparent, comprehensible categorization boundaries, aligning with domain expert expectations. Ultimately, our study illustrates that incorporating a semantic layer for document categorization illuminates the categorization process and facilitates more accurate predictions. MathBench and our code are publicly available at mathbench.github.io and github.com/roundedsquare/mathbench.

Existing evaluation metrics for summarization models are limited in several ways:
\emph{(1)} they do not consider what the model is actually doing -- how well the summary represents the original text -- because they only assess summaries via paraphrased, lexical similarity measures; \emph{(2)} they do not utilize structured data like abstracts to compute summary quality more accurately; \emph{(3)} they perform poorly in their generalization ability. To address these issues, a novel cross-encoder based external metric called SummScore is proposed, which determines the quality of a summary by measuring how strongly it connects to the corresponding part of the original text via a cross-encoder model. Unlike other metrics, SummScore assesses summaries using the entire original text, thereby providing more precise and comprehensive evaluations. Experimental findings with multiple state-of-the-art summarization models confirm the superiority of SummScore in terms of its ability to accurately predict human judgment, demonstrate its great potential in training summarization models to better utilize the relevant information in the original text, and ultimately outperform existing metrics. Additionally, SummScore offers a meaningful way to identify valuable structures in the original text that are worth quoting in the summary. We analyze a common signal recovery problem tied to a quadratic form derived from an observed vector and a known matrix. This type of problem, encompassing instances like noise reduction and equalization, can be complex to solve due to the quadratic nature. However, we limit our study to a specific subset of matrices containing real, positive, definite, symmetric elements. These matrices ensure the signal restoration problem has a single, optimal solution with a convex form, simplifying the analysis and computation. We apply the method of regularization to create an algorithm for the restoration task, tying it to a regularized version of the original problem. This method is analogous to standard approaches like Tikhonov regularization and is proven to the best approximation at a specified regularization level. We also discuss strategies for choosing the regularization parameter, including a approach based on minimum principles, that is demonstrated to be effective in real-world scenarios. We extend this method to address multi-dimensional signal recovery tasks and provide supporting examples and tests of the method's efficacy. We observe the method's performance compares favorably to other approaches such as MMSE when the correct noise level is known or when the noise level is estimated accurately. The impact of these disturbances on the dissipation process in the Ioffe paper's "dissipation range" is examined in detail. It is demonstrated that a significant number of high-frequency oscillations are required for their dissipation rate to significantly deviate from the classical value, with the magnitude of the dissipation constant being the product of the viscosity and the imaginary component of the frequency. An expression is also provided for the power spectrum of the thermal shift that takes into account the effects of these disturbances, with the spectrum exhibiting a power-law increase at low frequencies characterized by a specific exponent and incorporating the Thomson scattering length and Landau damping constants. At higher frequencies, the power-law increase continues with an altered exponent value, with which the dissipation constant and a constant comprising the dissipation length and a combination of the Landau parameters aligns. It is also noted that a component of the power spectrum exhibiting a power-law decrease with frequency may exist in this scenario. If such a component does exist, it would result in the power spectrum crossing over to a power-law increase at a specific threshold frequency, with which the dissipation constant and a combination of the Landau parameters, along with the length-scale of the turbulent flows, aligns. This additional component is attributed to the negative backflow effect caused by the dissipation of long-wavelength disturbances. With a subsequent integration of the resulting power-law decrease component, the power spectrum would contain two distinct parts: a power-law decrease component in the low-frequency range and a power-law increase component in the high-frequency range with which the dissipation constant and a combination of the Landau parameters and the length-scale of the turbulent flows aligns. In the design field, design dialogues offer valuable insights into users' problem-solving approaches and can be utilized for educational purposes. Effective mining of design dialogues requires the capacity to understand and interpret both the inherent design, as well as the social and cognitive aspects, of these dialogues. Consequently, designers and representatives of design organizations can learn from collected design dialogues, thereby improving future design processes. Nonetheless, the design dialogue mining process carries considerable costs in terms of time and resources; hence, the need to establish standards and best practices is paramount. We propose utilizing Natural Language Processing and Machine Learning to develop a framework for conclusion identification, as well as conclusion extraction and evaluation. This framework is foundational for the design dialogue mining process and serves as a crucial stepping stone towards conclusion-based ranking and summarization schemes. We evaluated and adapted the NLP and ML components, as well as the entire conclusion identification and extraction pipeline. Furthermore, we examined the robustness of conclusions derived from actual design dialogue datasets. Our findings indicate that the use of NLP and ML in design dialogue mining can be a reliable approach. Additionally, the conclusion robustness of results can be enhanced by incorporating methods for eliminating stop-words and incorporating the semantic meaning of words in the analysis, as well as by increasing the dataset size and quality. We obtained consistent results across various case studies, as well as within a case study that involved co-design among different stakeholders. Our study demonstrates that the combination of NLP and ML is a valuable tool for supporting the design dialogue mining process and showcases its potential as a data-driven approach for identifying and understanding user problem-solving strategies. As such, we expect this contribution to contribute significantly towards establishing standard and best practice protocols for design dialogue mining. Furthermore, the employed technological framework can be freely accessed and utilized by designers and design organizations, thereby streamlining the design dialogue mining process and yielding valuable datasets and knowledge bases. These datasets and knowledge bases can ultimately be integrated into organized libraries that are accessible to designers, researchers and organizations, thereby fostering knowledge sharing and collaboration. Our study expands the existing design dialogue mining boundaries by incorporating technological and data-driven principles. As a result, the employed technological framework may pave the way for further research on design dialogue mining and may eventually lead to the development of more sophisticated design dialogue mining tools and libraries. Such tools and libraries can be utilized for supporting the design process, as well as for promoting design thinking and thinking for design among various stakeholders. Our study has been recognized at the 2020 International Conference on Engineering and Multi-site Collaboration (EMSC)

However, deeply rooted traditions within the control community have led to discrepancies in understanding the nature and variability of neural networks when applied in control scenarios. These discrepancies result in a need for additional research to integrate neural networks within the frameworks provided by modern control theory. This paper aims to bridge these disparities by exploring the variability of neural networks when used for control purposes and providing a comprehensive overview of methods to validate such networks. We begin by examining the inherent properties of neural networks that affect their behavior when applied in control systems. We then delve into the theoretical underpinnings of validating neural networks, starting with the fundamental principles and expanding to more complex and intriguing aspects of the subject. A particular focus is placed on the applicability of neural networks in robust control systems and their potential use in dealing with uncertain systems through deep universal approximators. Additionally, we touch upon the future directions of neural network validation in the context of control theory. We also include an appendix that provides a concise and accessible introduction to validating neural networks in the context of estimation. Furthermore, we contribute substantively to validating neural networks by expanding the theoretical underpinnings of neural network validation in the context of control theory. Specifically, we provide a mathematical proof demonstrating that neural networks can be validated for infinite-time hysteretic feedback control in linear time-varying systems, even in the presence of hysteretic nonlinearity. We also introduce the concept of least-squares neural networks, which can be validated for finite-time hysteretic feedback control in linear time-varying systems. These contributions represent key advancements in the field of neural network validation in control theory. Clustering is a fundamental concept in data analysis, where the entire data set is partitioned into distinct subsets called clusters, ensuring that all points within a cluster are more similar to each other than those in separate clusters. Overlapping clustering is an extension of this concept, where points can belong to more than one group at a time. Traditional clustering frameworks often lack theoretical connections to other data analysis components, limiting their utility. This study introduces a novel method for creating overlapping clusters in a way that is consistent across multiple iterations. This approach builds upon a method called functorial clustering, providing a step-by-step procedure to create clusters at varying levels of granularity, all of which are interconnected. From the resulting hierarchy, any subset of data points can be grouped into clusters at various levels of specificity. Crucially, this method produces consistent results in a mathematical sense, facilitating a range of applications. An implementation of this method, including all underlying code, is now publicly accessible through the functorclustering Python package. Several examples demonstrate the method's ability to handle complex data sets effectively, including data with pre-existing groupings and data for predictive analysis with pre-specified categories. Additionally, the method is used to create a new taxonomy of flower species based on characteristcs from the Flora Catalana. Furthermore, the method is used to analyze the structure of the Wikipedia online database. Finally, the method is used to investigate the connections between the underlying structures of data sets with no initial grouping, revealing new patterns and relationships. All of these examples confirm the method's effectiveness in a wide array of applications. Additionally, the method's utility is demonstrated through applications to unsupervised feature extraction, generative modeling, and other advanced data analysis tasks. A public repository is available at https://functorclustering.github.io/. functorclustering exhibits over 20,000 unique page views and 7,000 daily active users from over 70 different countries. Furthermore, the method's utility is demonstrated through applications to unsupervised feature extraction, generative modeling and other advanced data analysis tasks. The source code for the method's implementation, including all underlying code, is now publicly accessible through the functorclustering GitHub page, where it has received over 150 individual contributions from 40 users, the majority of which are active developers. Deep learning has made significant advancements in the field of data recovery, but the development of efficient and streaming-friendly methods remains a challenge, particularly for 3D tensor data restoration. The Tensor Ring model has shown promise in compressing and recovering 3D data, but algorithms built around learning dense features often fail to accommodate the real-time requirements of streaming data. In response, we present a novel approach using the Patch Monitoring technique to enhance the restoration of visual data in a streaming environment. By integrating the Patch Monitoring mechanism into the update rule of TR-RDA, the proposed Patch Monitoring based Streaming Tensor Ring Restoration (PM-STRR) method achieves more accurate and efficient recovery results. Experiments conducted across various tasks, including tensor completion and compression, demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method, which further supports its efficiency and streaming-friendly design with empirical evidence and runtime comparisons. In particular, the proposed method improves recovery accuracy by 3.08 dB and 1.40 dB for NMT and DMC tasks, respectively, while reducing the model training time by nearly 10 times and the inference time by 20-30 times and enhancing the inference runtime by 2-3 times. Notably, the proposed method allows for direct deployment without fine-tuning, representing a 4,000 times speedup, and surpasses the state-of-the-art model, TR-RDA, with a margin of 1.98 dB.
